blocks.text: A view is a stored query. You hand the database a `SELECT` statement, give it a name, and from that point on the name can be used almost anywhere a table name is allowed. Nothing is copied. No second set of rows is written anywhere. The rows you see through a view still live in the tables underneath it.
**Start with the data:** the first view reads from `ITEM`. This is the complete base table before the `HABITAT` view filters its rows and columns.

blocks.caption: Base table: ITEM — the rows available to the first view

blocks.label: Three words you need
blocks.text: The **base tables** are the real tables the data lives in, such as `ITEM` and `CUSTOMER`. The **defining query** is the `SELECT` statement you stored. The **view** is the name you gave that query. A view has no rows of its own.
The syntax is short. You write `CREATE VIEW`, the name, the word `AS`, and then any `SELECT` statement you already know how to write.

CREATE VIEW view_name AS
SELECT column_list
FROM   table_list
WHERE  condition;

KimTay's `ITEM` table mixes four categories together. A buyer who only handles habitat products has to remember to add `WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat'` to every single query, and has to get it right every single time. A view removes that burden. Run this.

blocks.hint: The view returns AV07 and FT88. Notice the second query in the solution: once `HABITAT` exists you can put a `WHERE` clause on it exactly as if it were a table. That second query returns FT88 alone.

blocks.text: Two things just happened that are worth naming. The view narrowed the rows, keeping only the habitat items, and it narrowed the columns, dropping `CATEGORY` and `REORDER_LEVEL` from sight. Views can do either or both.

cards.title: Simplification
cards.body: A four-table join with a dozen conditions is hard to type and easy to get subtly wrong. Store it once as a view and every report after that is a plain `SELECT` from a single name. One query to review, one query to fix when the rules change.

cards.title: Showing only part of a table
cards.body: `CUSTOMER` holds credit limits. Counter staff need names and balances but have no business seeing credit limits. Build a view with only the permitted columns and give access to the view instead of the table. What is not in the view cannot be read through it.

blocks.text: A view is always current

This is the part that surprises people. The defining query is not run when you create the view. It is run every time you use the view. That means a view can never go stale. If somebody adds a habitat item to `ITEM` at four in the afternoon, the next person to select from `HABITAT` sees it. Watch it happen.

blocks.hint: Two items were inserted but the second `SELECT` from the view grows by only one row, from two to three. TR55 is a habitat item so it qualifies; CH12 is an accessory so the defining query's `WHERE` clause leaves it out. The view was never touched by the `INSERT` statements. It simply asked the question again.

blocks.label: About the numbers you see
blocks.text: This engine stores `DECIMAL` values as ordinary numbers, so a stored `42.50` is displayed as `42.5`, `85.00` as `85`, and `7500.00` as `7500`. The value is right; the trailing zeros are a formatting choice, not a change in the data.
Naming the view's columns

By default a view's columns inherit the names in the `SELECT` list. You can rename them by listing new names in parentheses after the view name. Do this when the base column names are cryptic, when two joined tables both contribute a column of the same name, or when a column is computed and would otherwise have no sensible name at all.

blocks.hint: The column headings come back as ID, ITEM_NAME, UNITS and UNIT_PRICE, with FT88 first and AV07 second. From here on, `ORDER BY PRICE` against this view fails with `no such column: PRICE`: outside the view those columns no longer answer to their old names.

blocks.text: A view over a join

This is where views start earning real money. Pulling an invoice line together with its item description and its customer name takes a four-table join. Nobody wants to retype that for the sales report, the reorder report and the collections report. Write it once.

blocks.starter:
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS INVOICE_DETAIL;

CREATE VIEW INVOICE_DETAIL AS
SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, I.INVOICE_DATE, C.CUSTOMER_NAME,
       T.DESCRIPTION, L.NUM_ORDERED, L.QUOTED_PRICE,
       ROUND(L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE, 2) AS LINE_TOTAL
FROM   INVOICE I
       INNER JOIN CUSTOMER C ON I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM
       INNER JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM
       INNER JOIN ITEM T ON L.ITEM_ID = T.ITEM_ID;

SELECT INVOICE_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, DESCRIPTION, LINE_TOTAL
FROM   INVOICE_DETAIL
WHERE  LINE_TOTAL > 50.00
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM, DESCRIPTION;
blocks.solution:
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS INVOICE_DETAIL;

CREATE VIEW INVOICE_DETAIL AS
SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, I.INVOICE_DATE, C.CUSTOMER_NAME,
       T.DESCRIPTION, L.NUM_ORDERED, L.QUOTED_PRICE,
       ROUND(L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE, 2) AS LINE_TOTAL
FROM   INVOICE I
       INNER JOIN CUSTOMER C ON I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM
       INNER JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM
       INNER JOIN ITEM T ON L.ITEM_ID = T.ITEM_ID;

SELECT INVOICE_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, DESCRIPTION, LINE_TOTAL
FROM   INVOICE_DETAIL
WHERE  LINE_TOTAL > 50.00
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM, DESCRIPTION;

SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, ROUND(SUM(LINE_TOTAL), 2) AS SPENT
FROM   INVOICE_DETAIL
GROUP BY CUSTOMER_NAME
ORDER BY SPENT DESC;
blocks.hint: The first query returns four lines over fifty dollars: 127.5, 85, 64.99 and 55.5. The solution adds a second, completely different question answered from the same view, with no join written a second time. That reuse is the whole point.

blocks.text: Notice `LINE_TOTAL`. A computed column needs a name, and the alias you give it in the defining query becomes a column of the view. Once the view exists, `LINE_TOTAL` can be used in a `WHERE` clause, in `ORDER BY`, and in `SUM`, as though the number were stored.
A view over grouped data
A view can also summarize. Group the invoice lines by invoice number, total them, and store that as a view. Everyone downstream now has invoice totals without knowing that `INVOICE_LINE` exists.

blocks.hint: Invoice 50710 comes to 151.48, invoice 50711 to 100.25 and invoice 50712 to 120.49. The second query filters on `TOTAL`, which in a direct query would have needed `HAVING`. Through the view it is an ordinary column, so a plain `WHERE` works. Remember the shape of this view: section 7-2c explains why a view built this way can never be written to.

blocks.label: A view is not a cache
blocks.text: Because the defining query runs on every use, a view built on an expensive join costs you that join every time. It buys clarity, not speed. Oracle offers materialized views, which really do store results and must be refreshed. MySQL and this engine have no such feature, so every view you write here is recomputed on demand.
Your turn

The starter below is deliberately unfinished, so it will not run until you complete it. Replace each `____` so the view holds every item priced above twenty dollars, then select from it in descending price order. Press Run, and check yourself against the solution.

blocks.hint: The condition goes in the defining query, not in the final `SELECT`. Three rows come back: AV07 at 64.99, CF21 at 42.5 and FT88 at 27.75.

I can explain that a view stores a query, not rows
I can say why a view is always current: the defining query runs on every use
I can rename a view's columns with a parenthesized list after the view name
I can build a view over a join and a view over `GROUP BY`
I can name the two reasons views exist: simplification, and showing a user only part of a table

sections.title: Using a View to Update Data

blocks.text: Reading through a view is easy. Writing through one is where the rules start. The question the database has to answer is always the same: if you change a row of the view, can it work out exactly which row of exactly which base table to change, with no guessing? When the answer is yes, the view is updatable. When the answer involves a guess, the update is refused.

blocks.label: Updatable view
blocks.text: A view is **updatable** when every row it produces maps back to one identifiable row in one base table, so that `UPDATE`, `INSERT` and `DELETE` against the view can be rewritten into the same operation against that base table. A view that summarizes, combines or collapses rows breaks that mapping.

blocks.label: Engine note - read this before you run anything
blocks.text: The sandbox on this page runs SQLite, which refuses **every** attempt to modify a view. `UPDATE HABITAT SET PRICE = 69.99 WHERE ITEM_ID = 'AV07';` comes back as `cannot modify HABITAT because it is a view`. MySQL is different: it accepts updates through views it judges updatable. So on this page the update attempts are MySQL code blocks, marked as such and not runnable here. Every sandbox shows the route that does run everywhere: change the base table, then select from the view and watch it change.
7-2a Updating row-and-column subset views

A row-and-column subset view draws from one base table, keeps a subset of its rows with a `WHERE` clause and a subset of its columns in the `SELECT` list, and does nothing else. No join, no `GROUP BY`, no aggregate, no `DISTINCT`. This is the one shape that is usually updatable, because each view row is one base row wearing fewer clothes.
Consider a view over the customers assigned to rep 20.

CREATE VIEW KAISER_CUST AS
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
FROM   CUSTOMER
WHERE  REP_NUM = '20';

That view returns two customers from the shipped data: 1120 Access Pet Center and 1310 Companion Care Clinic. In MySQL, raising the credit limit of Companion Care Clinic through the view works. MySQL rewrites the statement against `CUSTOMER`, adding the view's own condition to yours.

-- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
UPDATE KAISER_CUST
SET    CREDIT_LIMIT = 12000.00
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';
That is the happy case. Three things still go wrong often enough that you should expect them.

items: **Columns the view cannot see.** `KAISER_CUST` has no `REP_NUM` column, so an `INSERT` through the view has no way to supply one. In MySQL the new customer lands in `CUSTOMER` with `REP_NUM` left null - a null produced by that insert, not one present in any shipped row - and it is immediately invisible through the very view that created it. Had `REP_NUM` been declared `NOT NULL` with no default, MySQL in strict mode would reject the insert outright with error 1364.

**Rows that migrate out.** If a view filters on a column it also exposes, an update to that column can push the row out of the view. The update succeeds, the base row is fine, and the row vanishes from the user's screen.

**Required columns the view cannot reach.** An `INSERT` through a view can only supply the view's own columns. Every other column of the base table must be able to take a default or a null. A `NOT NULL` column with no default that the view omits - very often the primary key itself, since keys like `CUSTOMER_NUM` are not auto-generated - makes the insert impossible, and MySQL reports error 1364.

blocks.text: MySQL and Oracle both offer a guard against the migrating-row problem: add `WITH CHECK OPTION` to the view definition. Any change that would move a row out of the view is then rejected instead of quietly hiding it. SQLite has no `WITH CHECK OPTION`, so these two blocks are MySQL only.

-- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
CREATE VIEW BROOKVILLE_CUST AS
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY, BALANCE
FROM   CUSTOMER
WHERE  CITY = 'Brookville'
WITH CHECK OPTION;

-- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
UPDATE BROOKVILLE_CUST
SET    CITY = 'Northfield'
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

Without `WITH CHECK OPTION` that update succeeds and the row disappears from the view. With it, MySQL raises error 1369, a CHECK OPTION failure, and nothing changes. The sandbox below shows the disappearing act for real, by changing the base table instead.

blocks.hint: Whiskers & Wags Boutique is the only Brookville customer, so the view starts with one row and ends with none. The final query proves the row is still in `CUSTOMER`, alive and well, now showing Northfield. It stopped satisfying the defining query, that is all.

blocks.text: Now the other half of the base-table route. Watch a subset view pick up exactly the rows that belong in it, and ignore the ones that do not.

blocks.hint: Two customers were added to the base table and only one shows up in the view, which goes from two rows to three: 1550 belongs to rep 20, 1600 does not. Because the insert went to `CUSTOMER`, it could supply `REP_NUM`, which is precisely the column the view cannot reach.

blocks.text: 7-2b Updating views involving joins

A view over a join is usually not updatable, and the reason is worth understanding rather than memorizing. A single row of a join view is assembled from two or more base rows. Change something in that view row and the database has to decide which base row you meant. Worse, one base row can feed several view rows, so a change that looks like it touches one line on your screen may quietly touch several.

CREATE VIEW CUST_REP AS
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, C.BALANCE, R.LAST_NAME, R.RATE
FROM   CUSTOMER C
       INNER JOIN REP R ON C.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM;

MySQL will accept an update through this view **only** when the statement changes columns belonging to exactly one base table. The statement below qualifies, since `LAST_NAME` comes from `REP` alone. It succeeds, and it changes more than the person typing it expected.

-- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
UPDATE CUST_REP
SET    LAST_NAME = 'Kaiser-Wu'
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

The `WHERE` clause names one customer, so one view row looks targeted. But the update lands on rep 20's single row in `REP`, and rep 20 also serves Companion Care Clinic. Two rows of the view change. Run the base-table equivalent and see it for yourself.

blocks.hint: One row of `REP` changed. Two rows of the view changed: Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic, both served by rep 20, now show 0.06 while 1225 stays 0.07 and 1420 stays 0.05. That one-to-many fan-out is exactly the ambiguity that makes join views dangerous to write through.

blocks.text: Ask the join view to change columns from two base tables at once and MySQL stops cooperating altogether. The statement below touches `BALANCE`, which lives in `CUSTOMER`, and `LAST_NAME`, which lives in `REP`.

-- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
UPDATE CUST_REP
SET    BALANCE   = 4000.00,
       LAST_NAME = 'Kaiser-Wu'
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

MySQL rejects that with error 1393, `Can not modify more than one base table through a join view`. Oracle applies a related rule built on key-preserved tables: you may change columns of the one table whose primary key still uniquely identifies each row of the join, and nothing else. Different wording, same instinct.

blocks.caption: What each engine does with a write against a view
rows: UPDATE through a row-and-column subset view
Refused: cannot modify V because it is a view
Allowed, rewritten against the base table
INSERT or UPDATE through a join view
Allowed only when exactly one base table is touched
UPDATE through a GROUP BY view
Refused: target table is not updatable, error 1288

blocks.text: 7-2c Updating views involving statistics

A view built on aggregates is never updatable, in any engine, and there is no clever workaround. The reason is not a restriction someone chose to impose. It is that the number you want to change does not exist anywhere until the query computes it.

CREATE VIEW REP_BALANCE AS
SELECT REP_NUM,
       COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS,
       ROUND(SUM(BALANCE), 2) AS TOTAL_BALANCE
FROM   CUSTOMER
GROUP BY REP_NUM;
Rep 20's `TOTAL_BALANCE` is 3512.5, the sum of two customer balances: 3512.50 for Access Pet Center and 0.00 for Companion Care Clinic. Suppose someone tries to set it to 4000.

-- MySQL. Not runnable in the sandbox on this page.
UPDATE REP_BALANCE
SET    TOTAL_BALANCE = 4000.00
WHERE  REP_NUM = '20';

Which balance should move? Access Pet Center's, Companion Care Clinic's, or some split between them? There is no answer in the statement and no answer in the data. MySQL reports error 1288, `The target table REP_BALANCE of the UPDATE is not updatable`. A `DELETE` fares no better: deleting a summary row would mean deleting an unspecified number of customers.
The correct move is the one the data supports: change a real balance on a real customer, and let the view recompute. Run this and watch the total follow.

blocks.hint: Rep 20's total moves from 3512.5 to 4012.5 and the other two reps do not budge: 1200 for rep 35, 4820.75 for rep 65. You never wrote to the view. You wrote to one customer, and the aggregate recomputed on the next use, because that is what a view does.

blocks.label: The three questions
blocks.text: Before writing through a view, ask in order. **One table?** If the defining query names more than one table, expect refusal or surprise. **One row per row?** If `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT` or an aggregate collapses rows, the answer is no and the engine will say so. **Every required column reachable?** If a `NOT NULL` column with no default is missing from the view, an `INSERT` cannot succeed. Three yes answers and you probably have an updatable view. Any no, and the honest fix is to write to the base table.

items: I can define what makes a view updatable in one sentence about mapping to base rows
I can explain why a row-and-column subset view is usually updatable
I can describe the migrating-row problem and what `WITH CHECK OPTION` does about it
I can explain why a join view update can change more rows than the `WHERE` clause names
I can state the MySQL rule that a join view update may touch only one base table
I can give the real reason an aggregate view is never updatable, not just assert that it is
I can always fall back to updating the base table and reselecting from the view

blocks.text: When a view has outlived its usefulness, remove it with `DROP VIEW`. This is the least dramatic statement in the module, and the one students most often fear. Say the rule out loud once: `DROP VIEW` removes the stored query. It never removes data. It cannot remove data, because the view never held any.
DROP VIEW view_name;
Prove it rather than trusting it. The sandbox below builds a view of the cheaper items, confirms the view exists in the system catalog, drops it, and then goes looking for the data.

blocks.hint: The catalog lists SMALL_ITEM, then after the drop it lists nothing. The last two queries return the same three items the view was showing, DG04, FT88 and GR15, and confirm all five rows of `ITEM` are still there. The only thing that disappeared was the query.

blocks.label: One word apart, worlds apart
blocks.text: `DROP VIEW SMALL_ITEM;` costs you a definition you can retype in thirty seconds. `DROP TABLE ITEM;` costs you the company's product catalog. The statements look alike at three in the afternoon on a Friday. Read the second word before pressing Enter, and never test a `DROP` against production.

blocks.caption: What each statement takes away
rows: The HABITAT definition, now returning nothing
The ITEM table and all five rows

blocks.text: Two footnotes on that table. The middle row assumes foreign keys are not being enforced; with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` those two items are still quoted on invoice 50712, so the `DELETE` fails with `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. And the third row deserves a moment of its own. Dropping a base table does not drop the views built on it. The definition survives as an orphan and fails the next time somebody uses it, with `no such table: main.ITEM`. Cleaning up a table means cleaning up its views too.
DROP VIEW and IF EXISTS

Dropping a view that is not there is an error. In this engine the message is `no such view: NOPE`; MySQL reports error 1051, `Unknown table`. Both engines accept `IF EXISTS`, which turns the error into a shrug. That is why every sandbox in this module opens with `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS`: it lets you press Run twice without the second run failing on a name that is already gone.

DROP VIEW NOPE;            -- error: the view does not exist
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS NOPE;  -- no error, nothing to do
Views built on views

A view's defining query may name another view. That is convenient and it creates a dependency you have to remember when it is time to clean up. Drop the inner view and the outer one is left pointing at nothing.

blocks.hint: Only FT88 satisfies both filters, so `CHEAP_HABITAT` returns one row. Note that `CHEAP_HABITAT` filters on `CATEGORY`, a column it does not itself expose but which `CHEAP_ITEM` does. The drops run outermost first, VIEWS_LEFT is 0, and `ITEM` still has all five rows at the end.

blocks.text: Reverse the drop order and the database lets you do it. Neither this engine nor MySQL stops you from removing a view that another view depends on. The damage only shows up later, when somebody uses the survivor.

DROP VIEW CHEAP_ITEM;        -- succeeds
SELECT * FROM CHEAP_HABITAT; -- fails: no such table: main.CHEAP_ITEM

blocks.label: Before you drop anything
blocks.text: List what exists first. `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view';` shows every view in this engine. MySQL has no `sqlite_master`; there you would query `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS` instead. Reading the catalog costs one query and has saved a great many afternoons.

I can state without hedging that `DROP VIEW` never deletes data
I can tell `DROP VIEW`, `DELETE FROM` and `DROP TABLE` apart by what each one destroys
I know `IF EXISTS` prevents the no-such-view error and makes a script rerunnable
I know dropping a base table leaves its views behind, broken
I can list the existing views from the system catalog before I drop anything

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: creating and using views

questions.scenarioTitle: An overnight price change at KimTay
questions.stem: KimTay defines `HABITAT` as a view selecting item id, description, on hand and price from `ITEM` where the category is Habitat. Overnight a buyer changes the price of AV07 in the `ITEM` table. The next morning a clerk runs `SELECT * FROM HABITAT;`. What price does the clerk see for AV07?
options: The old price, because the view copied the ITEM rows at the moment it was created
An error message, because the view is now out of step with the table beneath it
The new price, because the defining query is run again every time the view is used
The new price, but only after someone runs a command to refresh the stored view
optionNotes: Treats a view as a snapshot of data. A view stores a query, never rows, so there is nothing to go out of date.
Assumes a view can become inconsistent with its base table. It cannot, since it reads that base table on every use.
Correct. The view has no rows of its own; the SELECT behind it executes fresh each time the view is named.
Confuses a plain view with an Oracle materialized view. Plain views in MySQL and SQLite have no refresh step.
questions.takeaway: A view is never stale because its defining query runs at the moment of use, not at the moment of creation.

questions.scenarioTitle: The four-table join in three reports
questions.stem: KimTay's sales, reorder and collections reports each retype the same four-table join across `INVOICE`, `INVOICE_LINE`, `ITEM` and `CUSTOMER`. A DBA proposes storing that join as the view `INVOICE_DETAIL`. Which benefit of the proposal is genuine?
options: Each report becomes a plain SELECT from one named view instead of restating the whole join
The joined result is written to disk once so the reports never have to read the base tables
The database begins refusing any report query that reaches the base tables directly
The four tables are merged into one permanent table sharing a single primary key
optionNotes: Correct. Simplification is the point: one definition to review, one place to fix when the join rules change.
Describes caching. A plain view stores no results, so every use pays for the join again.
Views do not restrict what other queries may do; only granted permissions can do that.
Nothing about the base tables changes. The view leaves all four tables exactly as they were.
questions.takeaway: A view buys clarity and reuse, not stored results and not enforcement.

questions.scenarioTitle: What the front counter may see
questions.stem: KimTay wants counter staff to read customer numbers, names and balances from `CUSTOMER`, but never credit limits. Which approach uses a view the way views are meant to be used?
options: Create the view, then delete the CREDIT_LIMIT column from CUSTOMER so nobody can reach it
Create a view over the whole CUSTOMER table and ask counter staff not to select CREDIT_LIMIT
Give the counter a nightly copy of CUSTOMER with the credit limit column left out of the copy
Create a view listing only the three permitted columns and give staff access to that view
optionNotes: Destroys data the business needs elsewhere. A view restricts what one group sees without changing the table.
A view that exposes every column protects nothing. Relying on people not to look is not access control.
A nightly copy is stale between refreshes and doubles the storage and the maintenance burden.
Correct. What the defining query omits cannot be read through the view, and the base table is untouched.
questions.takeaway: Showing a user only part of a table is a design goal you meet by narrowing the view's column list, not by changing the table.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: updating through a view

questions.scenarioTitle: Raising a credit limit at Companion Care Clinic
questions.stem: `KAISER_CUST` selects customer number, name, balance and credit limit from `CUSTOMER` where the rep number is 20. In MySQL a DBA runs `UPDATE KAISER_CUST SET CREDIT_LIMIT = 12000.00 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';`. What happens?
options: MySQL refuses it, since no view of any shape will ever accept an UPDATE statement
MySQL rewrites it as an update of the matching CUSTOMER row and the change succeeds
MySQL updates a copy of the data held inside the view and leaves CUSTOMER unchanged
MySQL updates every customer served by rep 20 because the view filters on rep number 20
optionNotes: Overgeneralizes from SQLite, which refuses all view writes. MySQL accepts writes to views it judges updatable.
Correct. This is a row-and-column subset of one table, so each view row maps to exactly one CUSTOMER row.
There is no copy inside a view. Any change that succeeds lands in the base table or nowhere.
The view's condition is added to your WHERE clause, not substituted for it, so only customer 1310 changes.
questions.takeaway: A row-and-column subset view is updatable because every view row traces back to one unambiguous base row.

questions.scenarioTitle: Adding Harbor Reef Supply through a partial view
questions.stem: `KAISER_CUST` exposes customer number, name, balance and credit limit, but not `REP_NUM`, which the `CUSTOMER` table permits to be null even though every shipped row has a rep. In MySQL a DBA inserts a new customer supplying values for the four view columns. What is the result?
options: The insert is rejected, since an INSERT must always supply a value for every base-table column
The row is inserted and appears in the view, since the view's filter is on rep number 20
The view's WHERE condition automatically supplies rep number 20 to the newly inserted row
The row lands in CUSTOMER with no rep number and is invisible through the view that created it
optionNotes: Columns you omit take their default or null. The insert is only rejected if an omitted column is NOT NULL with no default.
It cannot appear: with REP_NUM null the new row fails the view's condition immediately.
A WHERE clause filters rows; it never assigns values. WITH CHECK OPTION would reject the insert, not repair it.
Correct. The view cannot reach REP_NUM, so the new row misses the very condition that defines the view.
questions.takeaway: A column missing from a view is a column an INSERT through that view cannot supply, and the new row may vanish on arrival.

questions.scenarioTitle: Correcting a rep's name through CUST_REP
questions.stem: `CUST_REP` joins `CUSTOMER` to `REP` and shows the rep's last name beside each customer. In MySQL a DBA runs `UPDATE CUST_REP SET LAST_NAME = 'Kaiser-Wu' WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';`. MySQL allows it because only one base table is touched. What is the danger?
options: One REP row changes, so every customer served by that rep shows the new name in the view
Nothing at all changes, because a join view silently discards updates aimed at the second table
Only the view row for customer 1120 changes and the underlying REP table stays as it was
Rows in both CUSTOMER and REP are duplicated so the join can keep both spellings available
optionNotes: Correct. Rep 20 also serves Companion Care Clinic, so a WHERE clause naming one customer alters two view rows.
MySQL does not discard the update; it performs it against REP, which is exactly the problem.
A view has no rows to change on its own. The write reaches REP or it does not happen.
No engine duplicates base rows to resolve an update. The change lands on the single REP row.
questions.takeaway: One base row can feed many view rows, so an update through a join view can reach further than its WHERE clause suggests.

questions.scenarioTitle: Editing a rep's total balance
questions.stem: `REP_BALANCE` groups `CUSTOMER` by rep number and reports a customer count and the sum of balances. Rep 20's total is 3512.5. Why will no engine accept `UPDATE REP_BALANCE SET TOTAL_BALANCE = 4000.00 WHERE REP_NUM = '20';`?
options: Because any DECIMAL column produced by the SUM function is marked read-only by the engine
Because the view definition was written without adding the WITH CHECK OPTION clause to it
Because no single stored row holds that total, so there is nowhere to write the new value
Because a view containing GROUP BY has to be dropped and recreated before any change to it
optionNotes: The data type is irrelevant. The same refusal applies to COUNT, MIN and every other aggregate.
WITH CHECK OPTION guards migrating rows in a subset view; it has no bearing on aggregate views.

questions.scenarioTitle: Retiring the HABITAT view
questions.stem: KimTay no longer needs the `HABITAT` view, which showed AV07 and FT88 out of the five rows in `ITEM`. A DBA runs `DROP VIEW HABITAT;`. What is the state of `ITEM` afterwards?
options: AV07 and FT88 are deleted from ITEM along with the view definition that selected them
All five rows remain in ITEM; only the stored query named HABITAT has been removed
AV07 and FT88 are moved into a backup table so the habitat data can be recovered later
All five rows remain but ITEM stays read-only until an equivalent view is created again
optionNotes: A view holds no rows, so dropping it cannot remove any. This is the fear the statement's name invites and it is unfounded.
Correct. DROP VIEW removes a definition from the catalog and touches no data at all.
No engine creates a backup on DROP VIEW. There is nothing to back up.
Dropping a view places no restriction of any kind on the base table.

questions.scenarioTitle: Dropping the inner view first at KimTay
questions.stem: `CHEAP_HABITAT` is defined over `CHEAP_ITEM`, which is defined over `ITEM`. A DBA runs `DROP VIEW CHEAP_ITEM;` without touching `CHEAP_HABITAT` first. What happens?
options: CHEAP_HABITAT is dropped automatically as well, since its definition depended on CHEAP_ITEM
The DROP is refused and reports that CHEAP_HABITAT must be dropped before CHEAP_ITEM
Nothing breaks, because CHEAP_HABITAT copied its rows at the moment it was created
CHEAP_HABITAT survives as a definition and fails the next time somebody selects from it
optionNotes: Neither SQLite nor MySQL cascades the drop to dependent views; the orphan is left in the catalog.
No dependency check happens at drop time, which is precisely why the problem is easy to create.
Views never copy rows, so there is nothing stored to insulate CHEAP_HABITAT from the loss.
Correct. The drop succeeds quietly and the failure surfaces later as no such table: main.CHEAP_ITEM on the next use.
questions.takeaway: Dependencies are not enforced when you drop, so list your views first and remove the outermost one before the one it reads.

blocks.text: Everything you have written so far assumes the person at the keyboard is allowed to see everything. Real databases do not work that way. KimTay's shipping desk needs a customer's street and city to print a label. It has no business seeing what that customer owes or how much credit the company has extended. Security in SQL is the work of matching each account's access to the job that account actually does.

The DBMS is the right place to do that work. If you enforce the rule inside the application, anyone who reaches the data another way walks straight past it - a reporting tool, a command line, a second app written next year. A privilege granted in the DBMS holds no matter how the account arrives.

blocks.label: Privilege
blocks.text: A privilege is one action, on one database object, for one account: `SELECT` on `CUSTOMER`, `UPDATE` on `ITEM`. The DBA hands privileges out with `GRANT` and takes them back with `REVOKE`. Until some privilege is granted, an account can do nothing at all to that object.
Granting a privilege with GRANT

The shape of the statement reads like a sentence: `GRANT` the privilege `ON` the object `TO` the account. The account has to exist on the server already - `GRANT` hands out access, it does not create users.

After that statement, `shipping_clerk` can read `CUSTOMER` and do nothing else to it - no `INSERT`, no `UPDATE`, no `DELETE` - and still has no access at all to `ITEM`, `INVOICE`, or anything else. Privileges are additive: the account holds exactly what has been granted, one grant at a time. In MySQL an account name normally carries a host, so you will more often write `'shipping_clerk'@'localhost'`; Oracle uses the bare name.

blocks.label: Engine note: this whole section is MySQL and Oracle
blocks.text: SQLite has no user accounts, so it implements neither `GRANT` nor `REVOKE`. Run the first in a sandbox and you get `near "GRANT": syntax error`; run the second and you get `near "REVOKE": syntax error`. That is why every security statement on this page sits in a plain code block, never in a sandbox. Read them as MySQL and Oracle code - with one split flagged further down, where `PUBLIC` is Oracle only. The view work at the end of the section does run in SQLite, and you can execute all of it.

blocks.caption: The privileges you will grant most often
rows: Read rows from the table or view
The account that loads new `INVOICE_LINE` rows
A cleanup account that clears cancelled invoices
Every privilege the DBMS defines on that object
The owner of the `ITEM` catalog, and nobody else

blocks.text: You can list several privileges in one statement, and you can narrow `UPDATE` down to named columns. That last form is worth knowing: it lets one account change a customer's credit limit without touching the customer's balance.

blocks.label: ALL is a decision, not a shortcut
blocks.text: `GRANT ALL` is quick to type and hard to undo mentally - once several accounts hold it, nobody remembers who needs what. Grant the specific privileges the job requires. If you find yourself reaching for `ALL` because listing them is tedious, that is a sign the account may not need direct table access at all.
Granting to everyone: PUBLIC in Oracle, a role in MySQL

Some data really is for everyone. The `ITEM` catalog at KimTay is a fair example: every department needs to look up a description and a price, and nobody outside the buying team should change one. Oracle reserves an account name for exactly this case, `PUBLIC`, so you do not have to name account after account.

-- Oracle. PUBLIC is a reserved name meaning every account in the database.
GRANT SELECT ON ITEM TO PUBLIC;

MySQL has no `PUBLIC`. Type that same statement there and MySQL reads `PUBLIC` as an ordinary account name; since MySQL 8 will not create an account as a side effect of `GRANT`, the server rejects the statement instead of quietly granting anything. The MySQL way to say "everyone" is a role you grant to each account - and because a role is not active until it is made a default, that second statement matters as much as the first.

blocks.label: PUBLIC includes accounts that do not exist yet
blocks.text: In Oracle, a grant to `PUBLIC` covers every account in the database, including the ones somebody creates next year. It also means `REVOKE SELECT ON ITEM FROM temp_analyst;` accomplishes nothing on its own - that account still reads `ITEM` through the `PUBLIC` grant, and the `PUBLIC` grant is the one that has to go. Reserve `PUBLIC` for data you would be comfortable showing any employee.
Taking it back with REVOKE
`REVOKE` mirrors `GRANT` with one word changed: privileges are granted `TO` an account and revoked `FROM` one. The mismatch trips people up constantly, so read it out loud the first few times.

blocks.label: Revoking removes one path, not every path
blocks.text: An account can hold the same privilege through more than one route: a direct grant, an Oracle grant to `PUBLIC`, and in either engine a role it belongs to. Revoking the direct grant leaves the others standing - that is exactly the trap in the `PUBLIC` note above. When access has to end, check every route before you call the job done.
Views as a security mechanism

Here is the idea that ties this section to Module 7 as a whole. You do not have to choose between giving an account the whole table and giving it nothing. You can build a view that shows exactly the columns and rows the account should see, grant `SELECT` on the view, and grant nothing at all on the table underneath. The account cannot widen the view, because the `WHERE` clause and the column list live in the view definition rather than in the query the account writes.
Start with the column case. The shipping desk needs the mailing address and nothing financial.

blocks.hint: Add `STREET`, `CITY`, `STATE` and `ZIP` to the `SELECT` inside the view. All four customers come back, and there is no column in the result that could tell you what any of them owes. The `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS` line at the top is what lets you press Run as many times as you like.

blocks.text: With that view in place, the grant is one line, and it is the only access the shipping desk gets.

-- MySQL and Oracle only.
GRANT SELECT ON SHIPPING_CONTACT TO shipping_clerk;

A view hides rows just as well as it hides columns. Suppose the Brookville territory gets its own account, and that account should see only the customers of rep 65 - which in the shipped data is `1420`, Whiskers & Wags Boutique.

blocks.hint: `WHERE REP_NUM = '65'` belongs inside the view definition. Put it there and one row comes back. Writing it on the outer `SELECT` instead would show the same single row today, but it would be the account's own query doing the filtering - and an account can always delete its own `WHERE` clause. Inside the view, the restriction is not the account's to remove.

blocks.label: Engine note: changing data through a view
blocks.text: MySQL will let an account `UPDATE` a simple view like `SHIPPING_CONTACT` and pass the change through to `CUSTOMER`, which is why granting `UPDATE` on a view deserves the same care as granting it on a table. SQLite refuses: `UPDATE SHIPPING_CONTACT SET CITY = 'Akron' WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';` answers `cannot modify SHIPPING_CONTACT because it is a view`. That is why the statement is quoted here rather than put in a sandbox. Creating views and reading from them works the same way in both.

items: Give each account the smallest set of privileges its work requires, and stop there.
Grant on a view rather than the table whenever the account needs only some columns or some rows.
Reserve Oracle's `PUBLIC` for data any employee could see, and remember it reaches accounts created later.
In MySQL there is no `PUBLIC` - create a role, grant the privilege to the role, then grant the role.
Write the `REVOKE` on the day the access stops being needed, not at the next audit.
Check every route - direct grant, `PUBLIC`, role - before you declare an account's access removed.

blocks.text: Look up one word in the back of a textbook and you find the page in a second. Without that index you would turn every page. A database index works the same way: it is a separate structure the DBMS maintains, holding the values of one or more columns in sorted order along with a pointer to the row each value came from. When a query filters or sorts on those columns, the DBMS can walk the small sorted structure instead of reading every row in the table.

blocks.label: Index
blocks.text: An index is a database object built on one or more columns of a table, kept in sorted order, that lets the DBMS find matching rows without scanning the whole table. It holds no data of its own - drop it and every row is still there, exactly as it was.

Nothing is free. The index is a second copy of those column values, so it takes disk space. More important, it has to stay correct: every `INSERT`, every `DELETE`, and every `UPDATE` that touches an indexed column has to change the index too. That is the trade you are making each time you create one.

cards.title: What an index buys you
cards.body: Faster `WHERE` lookups on the indexed columns, faster `ORDER BY` on them, and faster joins when the join column is indexed. On a five-row table you will not notice. On a table with two million invoice lines, the difference between a scan and an index lookup is the difference between a report that runs and one that times out.

cards.title: What an index costs you
cards.body: Extra storage, and slower writes. A table with four indexes does five pieces of work on every insert instead of one. An index nobody uses is pure cost - it slows every load and returns nothing. That is why dropping an unused index is a real optimization, not housekeeping.

blocks.text: 7-5a Creating an index

You give the index a name, name the table, and list the columns in parentheses. The name matters only for dropping it later - no query will ever mention it. The same statement works in SQLite, MySQL, and Oracle.
KimTay's staff search `ITEM` by description all day, so that is the column to index. Run the sandbox and the catalog will show the new object sitting next to the table it belongs to.

blocks.hint: The starter creates one index and lists it - one row. The solution adds a second one on `CATEGORY`, so two rows come back. Both boxes drop both names first, which is what lets you flip between starter and solution and still get the count each one promises. The `NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'` filter hides the indexes SQLite built automatically for the primary keys - those are there whether you ask for them or not.

blocks.text: An index can cover several columns. `CREATE INDEX CUSTOMER_INDEX3 ON CUSTOMER (REP_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME);` sorts by `REP_NUM` first and by `CUSTOMER_NAME` within each rep, which is exactly the shape of a query that filters on one rep and sorts the results by name. Order matters: this index helps a query that filters on `REP_NUM` alone, and does very little for one that filters on `CUSTOMER_NAME` alone.

You can watch the DBMS change its mind. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` asks SQLite how it intends to run a query without running it. In the starter below the index line is commented out, and the plan says `SCAN CUSTOMER`. Uncomment it - that is the solution - and the plan becomes `SEARCH CUSTOMER USING INDEX CUSTOMER_INDEX3`.

blocks.hint: Without the index the plan reads `SCAN CUSTOMER` plus `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` - every row read, then sorted. With it, the plan reads `SEARCH CUSTOMER USING INDEX CUSTOMER_INDEX3 (REP_NUM=?)`, and the sort disappears because the index already holds the names in order. You are reading the plan here, not the two customers of rep 20 - `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` describes the query instead of running it.

blocks.label: Engine note: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN is SQLite's spelling
blocks.text: `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` is SQLite syntax, which is why it runs in the sandbox. MySQL asks the same question with `EXPLAIN SELECT ...;`, and Oracle with `EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT ...;` followed by `SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);`. All three print something different, and none of the three wordings is portable. The question you are asking never changes: did the optimizer choose the index, or read the whole table?

blocks.label: You never name an index in a query
blocks.text: Notice that the `SELECT` is identical in both runs. Indexes are chosen by the query optimizer, not requested by you. There is no `FROM CUSTOMER USING CUSTOMER_INDEX3` in standard SQL. Your job is to create the indexes that fit how the data is actually queried; the optimizer's job is to decide, query by query, whether using one beats reading the table.
7-5b Dropping an index

An index that the optimizer never chooses is costing you writes and space for nothing, so removing it is real work. `DROP INDEX` takes the index name. The data is untouched - the same rows are still in the table when the statement finishes, and every query still returns the same answer, just possibly by a slower route.

blocks.hint: Only `ITEM_INDEX1` is left in the catalog. The solution goes one step further and reads `ITEM` afterwards, so you get two result tables: the one-row catalog listing, then all five items. Dropping an index removes an access path, never data.

blocks.caption: Index statements across the three engines
rows: `SELECT name, tbl_name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index';`

blocks.text: That SQLite listing statement has no `NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'` filter on it, so run it as written and you also get the five `sqlite_autoindex_*` entries SQLite built for the primary keys of `REP`, `CUSTOMER`, `ITEM`, `INVOICE`, and `INVOICE_LINE`. The sandboxes on this page add the filter to keep the output to the indexes you created yourself.
7-5c Creating unique indexes

Add the word `UNIQUE` and the index does a second job. It still speeds up lookups, but it also refuses any `INSERT` or `UPDATE` that would put a duplicate value in the indexed column. This is how you enforce "no two of these may ever match" on a column that is not the primary key.

Take a barcode table for the warehouse scanners. Two items sharing a barcode would mean the wrong product goes in the box, so the rule has to live in the database rather than in whichever program happens to be doing the insert.

blocks.hint: The starter builds the table and the unique index and shows two rows. The solution adds a third row with a barcode nobody else has - `740039` - and it is accepted, because unique means no repeats, not no new rows. `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` at the top takes the index with the table, so both boxes start clean every Run.

blocks.text: Now prove the rule bites. The sandbox below is the same setup with one extra statement at the end: an insert that reuses `CF21`'s barcode. It is rejected, and the message names the index's column.

blocks.hint: The starter stops with `UNIQUE constraint failed: ITEM_BARCODE.BARCODE`, and the error is all you see - the rows before it were stored, but nothing is displayed because the run never reached a `SELECT`. That is the index doing its job: the bad row never reaches the table. Change the value, as the solution does, and the insert goes through and three rows come back.

blocks.text: One more thing to expect: you cannot create a unique index on a column that already contains duplicates. The DBMS checks the existing rows first and refuses to build an index it would immediately violate. `CITY` in the shipped `CUSTOMER` data holds Maple Grove twice, so the attempt fails; `CUSTOMER_NAME` holds four different values, so that one succeeds.

blocks.starter:
-- Maple Grove appears twice in CUSTOMER, so this is refused.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CUSTOMER_CITY_UNIQUE ON CUSTOMER (CITY);
blocks.hint: The starter fails with `UNIQUE constraint failed: CUSTOMER.CITY` because customers `1120` and `1310` are both in Maple Grove. Nothing is created, so you can press Run on it as often as you like. The solution indexes `CUSTOMER_NAME` instead, where all four values differ, and the index appears in the catalog.

blocks.label: The primary key is already covered
blocks.text: You never need a unique index on a primary key column - declaring the key made it unique, and most engines build the supporting index for you. Those are the `sqlite_autoindex_*` rows the sandboxes filter out. Reach for `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` for the other columns that must not repeat: a barcode, an email address, an external order reference.

items: Index columns that appear often in `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, or a join condition.
Leave small tables alone - scanning three `REP` rows is already as fast as it gets.
Count the writes before adding an index to a table that is loaded in bulk every night.
Use `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` when a non-key column must never repeat, and clean the duplicates out first or the index will not build.
Drop any index the optimizer never chooses; it costs writes and space and returns nothing.
Remember the name is only for `DROP INDEX` - queries never mention it.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's shipping desk
questions.stem: The shipping desk needs every customer's name and street address to print labels, and must never see `BALANCE` or `CREDIT_LIMIT`. The account `shipping_clerk` currently holds no privileges at all. Which approach gives the desk exactly what it needs and nothing more?
options: Grant SELECT on the whole CUSTOMER table and trust the desk to ignore the financial columns
Grant ALL on CUSTOMER now so the desk never has to request more access later
Create a view holding only the address columns, then grant SELECT on that view
Revoke SELECT on BALANCE from the account first, then grant SELECT on CUSTOMER
optionNotes: This puts the rule in a person's good intentions rather than in the DBMS, which is exactly what privileges exist to avoid.
ALL includes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on customer records - far beyond reading an address, and hard to unwind later.
Correct: the view fixes the column list, so a grant on the view cannot reach BALANCE or CREDIT_LIMIT at all.
REVOKE only removes a privilege that was granted, and this account holds none yet. A later table-level GRANT SELECT on CUSTOMER would carry every column with it regardless.
questions.takeaway: When an account needs part of a table, grant on a view that exposes that part and grant nothing on the table itself.

questions.scenarioTitle: A contractor leaves KimTay
questions.stem: A contractor account named `temp_analyst` was granted `SELECT` on `INVOICE` directly last month, and the contract has now ended. No `PUBLIC` grant and no role touches `INVOICE`, so the direct grant is the account's only route to it. Which statement removes that read access and disturbs nothing else?
options: REVOKE SELECT ON INVOICE FROM temp_analyst; which removes exactly that one read privilege
REVOKE SELECT ON INVOICE TO temp_analyst; because REVOKE mirrors the wording GRANT uses
DROP TABLE INVOICE; and rebuild it so the old privilege refers to nothing
GRANT NONE ON INVOICE TO temp_analyst; overwriting the earlier privilege with nothing
optionNotes: Correct: REVOKE names the privilege, the object, and the account it is being taken from - and because the direct grant is the only route here, that one statement really does end the access.
The keyword is FROM, not TO - privileges are granted to an account and revoked from one.
This destroys the three INVOICE rows and breaks the foreign key INVOICE_LINE depends on, all to solve an access problem that one statement solves.
There is no NONE privilege in SQL; you remove access with REVOKE, not by granting something empty.
questions.takeaway: `REVOKE privilege ON object FROM account;` is the mirror image of GRANT, with FROM in place of TO - and it ends the access only when the grant it names is the account's only route.

questions.scenarioTitle: The ITEM catalog goes company-wide
questions.stem: KimTay wants every account in its Oracle database - including accounts created next year - to be able to read `ITEM`, while nobody outside the buying team may change it. Which single statement fits?
options: GRANT ALL ON ITEM TO PUBLIC; so that nobody is ever blocked from doing their job
GRANT SELECT ON ITEM TO every_user; naming the built-in group that means everyone
GRANT SELECT ON PUBLIC TO ITEM; naming the object first and the recipient second
GRANT SELECT ON ITEM TO PUBLIC; which covers every current and future account at once
optionNotes: ALL hands INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the catalog to every account in the database, which is the opposite of the requirement.
There is no every_user group; Oracle's reserved name for all accounts is PUBLIC.
The order is reversed - ON names the object being protected and TO names who receives the privilege.
Correct: PUBLIC is Oracle's reserved name for all accounts, and the grant reaches accounts created afterwards too.
questions.takeaway: In Oracle, `PUBLIC` means every account, now and in future - use it for data any employee could reasonably see.

questions.scenarioTitle: The same rule on the MySQL server
questions.stem: KimTay now needs that same "everyone may read `ITEM`" rule on a MySQL server. The DBA types `GRANT SELECT ON ITEM TO PUBLIC;` and MySQL rejects it. Why, and what works instead?
options: MySQL spells the same keyword ALL_USERS, so swapping the one word makes the statement run
MySQL has no PUBLIC, so it reads PUBLIC as an ordinary account name it will not create; instead create a role, grant SELECT on ITEM to the role, and grant the role to each account
MySQL refuses any grant on a table that already carries a primary key index, so the index has to be dropped first
MySQL requires a privilege to be revoked before it can be granted, so REVOKE SELECT ON ITEM FROM PUBLIC has to run first
optionNotes: There is no ALL_USERS keyword in MySQL either; the mechanism is missing, not the spelling.

Correct: PUBLIC is Oracle's. MySQL 8 will not create an account as a side effect of GRANT, so it errors, and a role granted to every account is the equivalent - remember SET DEFAULT ROLE, since a role is inactive until it is made a default.
Primary key indexes have nothing to do with privileges; every KimTay table has one and grants work fine.
Nothing has to be revoked before it is granted, and REVOKE against a non-existent PUBLIC account fails for the same reason the GRANT did.
questions.takeaway: `PUBLIC` is Oracle's; in MySQL you reach every account with a role that you grant out and set as a default.

questions.scenarioTitle: The nightly INVOICE_LINE load
questions.stem: KimTay's nightly job inserts several hundred rows into `INVOICE_LINE`, and the table is read by exactly one month-end report that totals every row in it. A developer proposes adding four new indexes to the table. What should you expect?
options: The inserts get faster, because each index gives the DBMS a shorter path to the new row
The nightly inserts slow down, because every index must be updated for each new row
Nothing measurable changes, since an index occupies space but never affects write speed
The month-end report speeds up sharply, because a full scan always uses the newest index
optionNotes: An index is extra work on insert, not a shortcut - the DBMS still has to place the row and then update each index.
Correct: four indexes mean five structures to maintain per inserted row, which is the cost side of the trade.
Maintaining an index on every write is precisely where the cost shows up; space is the smaller half of it.
A report that reads every row gains nothing from an index, because there is no subset to find.
questions.takeaway: An index trades slower writes and extra space for faster reads - on a write-heavy, scan-once table you pay the cost and collect nothing.

questions.scenarioTitle: Barcodes in the KimTay warehouse
questions.stem: Warehouse staff scan a six-character barcode stored in a table alongside `ITEM_ID`. Two different items must never carry the same barcode, but the barcode is not that table's primary key. Which action enforces the rule inside the DBMS?
options: Add an ordinary CREATE INDEX on the barcode column, which speeds lookups and blocks repeats
Have the application check for a matching barcode before every insert, then insert the row
Nothing can be done, because only a primary key column can be kept unique in SQL
Create a unique index on the barcode column so a duplicate value is rejected on insert
optionNotes: An ordinary index happily stores the same value many times; only the UNIQUE keyword refuses duplicates.
A check in one program does not bind the next program, the reporting tool, or a hand-typed INSERT.
Uniqueness can be enforced on any column with a unique index, key or not.
Correct: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX makes the DBMS itself refuse the second row with UNIQUE constraint failed, whatever tool sends it.
questions.takeaway: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` is how you enforce no-duplicates on a column that is not the primary key.

questions.scenarioTitle: Dropping ITEM_INDEX2
questions.stem: An index named `ITEM_INDEX2` on `ITEM (CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION)` is never chosen by the optimizer, so the DBA runs `DROP INDEX ITEM_INDEX2;`. What happens to KimTay's data and queries?
options: All five ITEM rows remain untouched, and queries return the same answers, possibly more slowly
Every row the index pointed at is deleted along with the index structure itself
The CATEGORY and DESCRIPTION columns are removed from ITEM by the drop
Queries that name ITEM_INDEX2 in their FROM clause now fail with an unknown object error
optionNotes: Correct: an index holds no data of its own, so dropping it removes only an access path.
The index stores pointers to rows, not the rows - removing it cannot remove data.
That would be ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN; DROP INDEX does not change the table's structure.
No query ever names an index in its FROM clause, so no query can break when one disappears.
questions.takeaway: Dropping an index removes an access path and nothing else - the rows, the columns, and the answers all stay the same.

questions.scenarioTitle: Making the optimizer use CUSTOMER_INDEX3
questions.stem: After creating `CUSTOMER_INDEX3` on `CUSTOMER (REP_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME)`, a developer asks what has to change in the next query so that the new index actually gets used. What is the right answer?
options: Add the index name to the FROM clause, the way a second table would be listed there
Rewrite the query as a subquery, since the optimizer consults indexes only for nested SELECTs
Write the query normally against CUSTOMER; the optimizer decides whether the index helps
Grant SELECT on the index to the account running the query, or the index stays unused
optionNotes: Standard SQL has no syntax for naming an index in a query - the FROM clause names tables and views.
Nesting has nothing to do with index selection; the optimizer weighs every access path in every query.
Correct: you create indexes to fit the workload, and the optimizer picks one query by query - EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN is how you check which way it went.
Indexes are not objects you grant privileges on; access is controlled on the table or view.
questions.takeaway: You choose which indexes exist; the optimizer chooses when to use them, and the query text never changes.

blocks.text: Every database you have built in this course knows something about itself. When you ran `CREATE TABLE ITEM`, the DBMS did not only make room for rows. It also wrote down that a table called `ITEM` exists, that it has six columns, that `ITEM_ID` is four characters and is the primary key, and that `REORDER_LEVEL` holds a small integer. That record lives inside the database, in tables you can read with an ordinary `SELECT`. It is called the system catalog, and it is what lets a DBMS answer questions about its own contents.

blocks.label: System catalog
blocks.text: A set of tables the DBMS maintains about the database itself: which tables, columns, views, and indexes exist, and how each one is defined. It is also called the data dictionary. You read it with `SELECT`; you never write to it directly.

The catalog earns its keep on the job for three reasons. You will inherit databases you did not build and have to find out what is in them. You will need to know what a change is going to break before you make it, and the only reliable list of everything that stores a `REP_NUM` is the catalog. And the tools you already use are reading it for you: the schema strip on every sandbox on this page, the object list in MySQL Workbench, the migration script your team runs on a Friday afternoon.
What the catalog can tell you

items: Which tables exist in the database, and on the larger engines who owns them
Which columns each table has, in what order, of what type, and whether nulls are allowed
Which views exist, and the defining query stored with each one
Which indexes exist and which table and columns they were built on
Which constraints are declared, including primary keys and foreign keys
On MySQL and Oracle, which users hold which privileges on which objects

blocks.text: MySQL: INFORMATION_SCHEMA

MySQL exposes the catalog as a database named `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` whose tables you query like any other. Two of them do most of the work. `TABLES` holds one row per table, and `COLUMNS` holds one row per column of every table. Both are filtered by `TABLE_SCHEMA`, which is the name of the database you are asking about. Leave that filter off and you get every database on the server, which is almost never what you meant.

-- MySQL. INFORMATION_SCHEMA does not exist in SQLite, so neither of these runs on this page.
SELECT TABLE_NAME
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY'
ORDER BY TABLE_NAME;

SELECT COLUMN_NAME, DATA_TYPE, CHARACTER_MAXIMUM_LENGTH, IS_NULLABLE
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY'
  AND TABLE_NAME = 'REP'
ORDER BY ORDINAL_POSITION;

MySQL also gives you `SHOW TABLES;` and `DESCRIBE REP;`, which are short-hand for those same two queries. They are convenient at a command line and useless inside a program, because a `SHOW` result cannot be joined, filtered, or counted. Anything you want to compute with has to come from `INFORMATION_SCHEMA`.

blocks.caption: Asking the same four questions of three engines
rows: SELECT TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY';
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table';
SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY' AND TABLE_NAME = 'REP';
SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM USER_TAB_COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_NAME = 'REP';
SELECT TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY';
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view';
SELECT DISTINCT INDEX_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.STATISTICS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY';
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index';

blocks.text: SQLite: sqlite_master and pragma_table_info

SQLite has no `INFORMATION_SCHEMA`. It keeps one catalog table, `sqlite_master`, holding a row for every table, view, index, and trigger in the database. The columns you will use are `type`, `name`, `tbl_name` (the object the entry belongs to), and `sql` (the exact statement that created it). Run the starter first, then narrow it.

blocks.solution:
SELECT type, name
FROM sqlite_master
WHERE type IN ('table', 'view')
ORDER BY type, name;
blocks.hint: The unfiltered version also lists the indexes SQLite built on its own. Add a `WHERE` clause on `type` to keep tables and views only.

blocks.text: The starter returns ten rows: the five KimTay tables and five entries of type `index` whose names begin `sqlite_autoindex_`. Nobody typed a `CREATE INDEX` for those. SQLite built one for each primary key so it could enforce uniqueness, and it recorded them in the catalog exactly as faithfully as the objects you asked for. The filtered version comes back with the five tables and no views, because this database has none yet.
For columns, SQLite offers `pragma_table_info`, a function you put in a `FROM` clause and hand a table name. It returns one row per column, in table order.

blocks.hint: `notnull` is a keyword in SQLite, so it has to be wrapped in double quotation marks before the engine will read it as a column name.

blocks.text: Nine rows come back in the order the columns were declared. Any column the `CREATE TABLE` declared `NOT NULL` shows a `notnull` of `1`; in `REP` those are `LAST_NAME` and `FIRST_NAME`, because a rep with no name is not a rep. `pk` reads `1` on `REP_NUM`, marking it as the first column of the primary key. Run the same query against `INVOICE_LINE` and you get `1` on `INVOICE_NUM` and `2` on `ITEM_ID`, which is how a two-column key is recorded.

blocks.label: One reading that will surprise you
blocks.text: `REP_NUM` is the primary key, yet its `notnull` value is `0`. In MySQL and Oracle a primary key column is automatically `NOT NULL`, and their catalogs say so. SQLite is the exception, and section 7-7 shows exactly what that lets through the door.
The question only the catalog can answer

KimTay asks you to widen `REP_NUM` from two characters to three. Before you touch anything you need the list of every table that stores a `REP_NUM`. No query against the data can produce that list, because you would have to know where to look before you could look. The catalog produces it in one statement.

-- MySQL: one row per column of every table, so a column name is searchable.
SELECT TABLE_NAME
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY'
  AND COLUMN_NAME = 'REP_NUM'
ORDER BY TABLE_NAME;

blocks.starter:
SELECT m.name AS TABLE_NAME
FROM sqlite_master m
WHERE m.type = 'table'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pragma_table_info(m.name) c WHERE c.name = 'PRICE')
ORDER BY m.name;
blocks.solution:
SELECT m.name AS TABLE_NAME
FROM sqlite_master m
WHERE m.type = 'table'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pragma_table_info(m.name) c WHERE c.name = 'REP_NUM')
ORDER BY m.name;
blocks.hint: The starter searches for `PRICE` and finds one table. Change the column name to `REP_NUM` and run it again.

blocks.text: `PRICE` lives in `ITEM` alone. `REP_NUM` lives in `CUSTOMER` and `REP`, so the widening job is two `ALTER TABLE` statements and not one. Because `pragma_table_info` accepts the table name from the outer query, the subquery runs once per table, and the answer stays correct when somebody adds a sixth table next month.
7-6a Update of the System Catalog

Nobody keeps the catalog current by hand. The DBMS updates it as part of carrying out the statement you ran. `CREATE TABLE` adds the rows that describe the new table, `CREATE INDEX` adds a row for the index, `DROP TABLE` removes every row belonging to that table, and `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO` rewrites the stored definition under the new name. All of it happens inside the same statement, so the catalog is never out of step with the database it describes.
You can watch it happen. Count the catalog, create something, count it again.

blocks.hint: Nothing in this script writes to `sqlite_master`. Every change to it is a side effect of `CREATE` and `DROP`. The `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` on line 1 is what lets you press Run twice.

blocks.text: The starter reports ten entries before and twelve after, because it created a table and SQLite quietly added the index that enforces its primary key. The solution asks for a second index as well, so it reports thirteen, and its middle result lists all three entries side by side. Then one `DROP TABLE` takes the count back to ten, because dropping a table removes the catalog entries for its indexes as well. You never wrote a single `INSERT` or `DELETE` against the catalog.

blocks.label: Read the catalog; never write to it
blocks.text: `sqlite_master` is a real table, and `UPDATE sqlite_master SET name = 'ITEMS';` looks like it should work. Do not. SQLite refuses it outright with `table sqlite_master may not be modified` unless a dangerous pragma is set, MySQL refuses it too, and on an engine that allows it you end up with a database whose description no longer matches its contents, which is how a file becomes unopenable. The way to change what the catalog says is to run the statement that changes the thing it describes.

cards.title: What the catalog is good for
cards.body: Finding your way around an unfamiliar database, listing every place a column name appears, confirming that a `CREATE` or `DROP` did what you expected, and generating scripts. Because the entries are rows, you can filter, join, count, and order them like any other data.

cards.title: What it is not
cards.body: It is not a backup and not a place to store notes about the database. It holds structure, not rows: the catalog knows `CUSTOMER` has a `BALANCE` column of type `DECIMAL(9,2)`, and knows nothing whatever about Whiskers and Wags Boutique owing 4820.75.

blocks.text: A constraint is a rule about what data is allowed, written into the table definition and enforced by the DBMS. That last part is what makes it worth the trouble. You can check in your own program that nobody enters a negative price, and the check protects the one program you wrote it in. Put the rule in the table and it protects the data against every program, every import script, every person at a command line, permanently.

blocks.label: Integrity constraint
blocks.text: A rule stored with the table that the DBMS applies to every insert, update, and delete. A statement that would break the rule is rejected with an error and nothing at all is changed.

You have been declaring constraints since Module 3 without dwelling on them. Every `CREATE TABLE` in the KimTay schema names a `PRIMARY KEY` and marks some columns `NOT NULL`, and the three tables with a parent above them (`CUSTOMER`, `INVOICE`, and `INVOICE_LINE`) declare `FOREIGN KEY` clauses as well. This section takes the whole set seriously: what each one refuses, what the refusal looks like, and which engine enforces which rule and when.
The five constraints

blocks.caption: The constraints SQL gives you
rows: Identifies each row uniquely. Values may not repeat, and on every engine except SQLite may not be null.
No two rows may hold the same value, but the column is still allowed to be null.
A supplier's email address: one address belongs to one supplier
The column must hold a value. A null is refused.
`LAST_NAME` in `REP`; a rep with no surname is not a rep
An expression that has to be true for the row. Anything false is refused.
A commission `RATE` has to fall between 0 and 0.25
A value here must already exist in the parent table's key. This is referential integrity.
`INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID` has to name an item that exists

blocks.text: A primary key is a unique constraint and a not-null constraint at the same time, plus the declaration that this is the identifier for the row. `UNIQUE` is the weaker relative you reach for when a second column also has to be one of a kind but is allowed to be missing.
Declaring them in CREATE TABLE

Constraints are declared where the table is defined. A rule about a single column can be written on that column's line. A rule about more than one column, or one you want to give a name to, goes on its own line after the columns. Naming a constraint with the `CONSTRAINT` keyword costs one word and buys you an error message that says which rule you broke.

CREATE TABLE SUPPLIER (
    SUPPLIER_ID    CHAR(3)      PRIMARY KEY,
    SUPPLIER_NAME  VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,
    EMAIL          VARCHAR(40)  UNIQUE,
    LEAD_DAYS      SMALLINT     NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT LEAD_DAYS_POSITIVE CHECK (LEAD_DAYS > 0)
);

blocks.hint: Add the named `CHECK` as a line of its own after `LEAD_DAYS`, then a second supplier, then read the catalog entries the table produced.

blocks.text: Two suppliers come back. The catalog query is the point where 7-6 and 7-7 meet: `SUPPLIER` produced three entries, the table plus two automatic indexes named `sqlite_autoindex_SUPPLIER_1` and `sqlite_autoindex_SUPPLIER_2`. One enforces the primary key and the other enforces the `UNIQUE` on `EMAIL`. A uniqueness rule is not a note in a manual; it is a structure the engine builds and maintains for you.
What a violation looks like

KimTay's warehouse tries to add a supplier that promises same-day delivery and records the lead time as zero days. Zero is not greater than zero, so the `CHECK` refuses the row. Run the starter as it stands and read the message. The sandbox shows you the error and nothing else, because the statement that failed stopped the script where it stood.

blocks.hint: The starter is meant to fail, so read the message before you change anything. Then give the rule the smallest lead time it will accept and run it again.

blocks.text: The engine answers `CHECK constraint failed: LEAD_DAYS_POSITIVE`. That is what naming the constraint bought you. Leave the name off and SQLite reports the expression instead, as in `CHECK constraint failed: LEAD_DAYS > 0`, and some engines report only the table, which tells you a rule was broken but not which one. The solution changes the zero to a one, the smallest lead time this rule allows, and both suppliers go in. The other three refusals read the same way, and every one of them names the column it protected.

blocks.label: A rejected statement changes nothing
blocks.text: The row is not written halfway. The `INSERT` is undone completely, the table is exactly as it was, and if you were inside a transaction the rest of it is still yours to `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. That is the whole promise of a constraint: the database never holds data that breaks its own rules, not even for an instant.
Referential integrity, enforced for real

Referential integrity is the rule that a foreign key has to point at a row that exists. `INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID` is declared `REFERENCES ITEM(ITEM_ID)` in the schema this page ships, so a line for item `ZZ99` ought to be impossible. Watch what actually happens.

blocks.starter: PRAGMA foreign_keys;
blocks.hint: Ask the engine for the current setting first, then try the insert it should have stopped.

blocks.text: The pragma reports `0`, and the insert is accepted. That is the explanation for both. SQLite parses foreign key declarations and stores them in the catalog, but it does not enforce them unless enforcement is turned on for the connection. The row you created is an orphan, an invoice line for an item that does not exist, and every inner join to `ITEM` will quietly leave it out: seven rows in `INVOICE_LINE`, six rows in the join. That is the shape of the bug, and it is a hard one to see.
Now turn enforcement on and run the identical insert.

blocks.starter:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
PRAGMA foreign_keys;
blocks.solution:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
INSERT INTO INVOICE_LINE VALUES ('50710', 'ZZ99', 1, 9.99);
blocks.hint: The starter proves the switch flipped: it reports `1` instead of `0`. Then add the same insert as the sandbox above and watch it be refused.

blocks.text: `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. Nothing was written. The engine looked for `ZZ99` in `ITEM`, did not find it, and refused the row, not because a program remembered to check but because the rule is in the database. Every route into the table is covered by it at once.
The rule guards the other direction as well. A parent row that children point at cannot be deleted out from under them.

blocks.solution:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
DELETE FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21';
blocks.hint: `CF21` is the grain-free dry food. The starter shows you which invoices ordered it; decide what should happen before you run the delete.

blocks.text: The starter returns two lines, on invoices 50710 and 50711. Removing the item would leave both pointing at nothing, so the engine refuses the delete with `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. Deleting those two lines first and then the item works. So does declaring the foreign key with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, which tells the engine to remove the children along with the parent. That is powerful and worth knowing, and worth respecting, because one short `DELETE` can then remove a great deal more than you had in mind.

blocks.label: The pragma is per connection, not per database
blocks.text: `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` lasts for the current connection and is not stored in the file. Press Reset on the sandbox, or open the same database from another program, and enforcement is off again. MySQL with InnoDB and Oracle enforce foreign keys always, with no switch anyone can forget. Expect inserts that passed on this page to start failing when you move the work to MySQL, and be glad of it: the ones that fail were the ones building orphans.
Enforcement does not get in the way of correct work. Item `DG04` exists, invoice `50712` exists, and the pair `(50712, DG04)` is not yet taken, so this row is legal with the pragma on.

blocks.hint: The starter shows the two lines invoice 50712 shipped with. Add the leash and three lines should come back.

blocks.text: PRIMARY KEY does not imply NOT NULL in SQLite

Here is the trap section 7-6 pointed at when `notnull` read `0` for `REP_NUM`. In MySQL and Oracle a primary key column is automatically `NOT NULL`; the engine adds the rule whether you write it or not. SQLite, for compatibility with databases written before the rule was enforced, lets a null into the primary key column of an ordinary table.

blocks.hint: This is a scratch table of your own, not KimTay's data, which ships with no nulls anywhere. Count the rows and count the keys separately, and Module 5 explains why the two numbers can differ.

blocks.text: One row stored, zero keys stored. `COUNT(*)` counts rows and `COUNT(REP_NUM)` skips the null, so the table holds a rep that nothing can identify or join to. The fix is two words in the right place. Write `REP_NUM CHAR(2) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY` and the same insert is refused with `NOT NULL constraint failed: REP_PRACTICE.REP_NUM`. It costs nothing on the engines that would have added the rule for you, so make it a habit.
Adding a constraint to a table that already exists

Everything above was declared at creation time. Real work is rarely that tidy: the `CHECK` you needed becomes obvious a year after the table went into production. MySQL 8.0 and Oracle let you attach one to a live table.

SQLite has no `ADD CONSTRAINT` at any version. Its `ALTER TABLE` expects a column definition after `ADD`, so it stops on the keyword `CONSTRAINT` and reports a syntax error there. A constraint has to be present when the table is created, so adding one means the rebuild pattern from 6-8a: create a replacement table with the constraint declared, copy the rows across, drop the original, rename the replacement, all inside one transaction. Exercise 5 walks that through on `REP`.

blocks.label: Check the data before you add the rule
blocks.text: A constraint added to a table that already has rows is accepted only if the existing data obeys it. One item priced at `0.00` and `ADD CONSTRAINT PRICE_POSITIVE` fails on MySQL, and the copy `INSERT` fails on SQLite. That is correct and useful behaviour. Run the query that finds the offenders first: `SELECT * FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE <= 0;` returns no rows on the shipped data, so the rule is safe to add here.
