blocks.text: Module 7 was about the work that surrounds the data rather than the data itself: what other people are allowed to see, how quickly the engine can find a row, what the database knows about its own shape, and which rules it will refuse to break. None of it changes a single value in `CUSTOMER`. All of it decides whether the values in `CUSTOMER` can be trusted and whether the database can be maintained by somebody who did not build it.
Views

A view is a query stored under a name and used as if it were a table. It holds no data of its own; the defining query runs every time the view is used, which is why a view is never out of date. Views give a user a row-and-column subset of a table, simplify a join that people would otherwise rewrite by hand, and hide columns nobody outside the office should see. On this page you can create a view and select from it. You cannot update through one, because SQLite answers `cannot modify V because it is a view`. MySQL permits it for simple views.
Security

`GRANT` gives a named user a specific privilege on a specific object, and `REVOKE` takes it back. The privilege is narrow on purpose: `SELECT` on one table, or `UPDATE` on one column, rather than the run of the database. Combine it with a view and you can let somebody read three columns of `CUSTOMER` and nothing else. Neither statement exists in SQLite at all, so both are MySQL and Oracle material, and both are examinable.
Indexes

An index is a structure the DBMS keeps so it can find rows by a column value without reading every row. `CREATE INDEX` builds one, `DROP INDEX` removes it, and the optimizer decides when to use it; you never name an index in a `SELECT`. Indexes cost space and slow down every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` that has to maintain them, which is why you index the columns you search and join on rather than all of them. A unique index also refuses duplicates, the same work a `UNIQUE` constraint does.
The system catalog

The catalog is the database describing itself. MySQL exposes it as `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES`, `.COLUMNS`, `.VIEWS`, and `.STATISTICS`; SQLite exposes `sqlite_master` and `pragma_table_info`; Oracle uses `USER_TABLES` and `USER_TAB_COLUMNS`. The DBMS updates it as part of every `CREATE`, `ALTER`, and `DROP`, so it is never stale. Read it freely and never write to it.
Integrity constraints

`PRIMARY KEY`, `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK`, and `FOREIGN KEY` are rules the DBMS enforces on every statement, from every program, forever. Declare them in `CREATE TABLE`. On SQLite, turn foreign keys on with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` per connection; MySQL and Oracle enforce them always. And remember the one SQLite lets through: a primary key column is not automatically `NOT NULL`, so write it.

blocks.starter: SELECT COUNT(*) AS CATALOG_ENTRIES FROM sqlite_master;
blocks.hint: The starter counts the ten entries the shipped database already has. Build one view and one index, then ask the catalog what you built. Both `DROP ... IF EXISTS` lines are there so you can press Run twice.

blocks.text: Three of this module's five themes in one short script. The view and the index both show up in the catalog the moment they exist, and the view returns Whiskers and Wags Boutique, Access Pet Center, and Downtown Aquarium and Pets, the three customers with a balance over 1000. Companion Care Clinic sits at 0.00 and stays out of it.

blocks.label: The habit to carry forward
blocks.text: When you can put a rule in the database instead of in a program, put it in the database. Applications get rewritten, replaced, and bypassed; the table outlives all of them. The same instinct applies to the catalog: before you change a column, ask the database what depends on it rather than trusting your memory of the schema.

blocks.text: These are the terms from Module 7 that come back in later work and on exams. The third column says where in the module each one was doing real work, so you know which sandbox to return to.

blocks.caption: Module 7 key terms, part one: views, security, and indexes
rows: A query stored under a name and used as if it were a table. It stores no rows of its own.
The `SELECT` a view is built from. The DBMS runs it again every time the view is used.
Views, why a view is never stale
A view that exposes some rows and some columns of one table and hides the rest.
Views, showing a clerk part of a table
A view you can change data through. MySQL allows it for simple views; SQLite refuses with `cannot modify V because it is a view`.
Statements that give a user a privilege on an object and take it away again. MySQL and Oracle only.
One specific right, such as `SELECT` on `CUSTOMER`, held by one specific user.
A structure the DBMS keeps so it can find rows by a column value without reading them all.
The statements that build and remove an index. You never name an index inside a `SELECT`.

blocks.caption: Module 7 key terms, part two: the catalog and the rules
rows: The tables in which the DBMS records what tables, columns, views, and indexes exist. Also called the data dictionary.
MySQL's catalog, queried through `TABLES`, `COLUMNS`, `VIEWS`, and `STATISTICS`. Absent in SQLite.
SQLite's single catalog table: one row per table, view, index, and trigger, with the `sql` that created it.
A SQLite function returning one row per column of a named table, with type, `notnull`, and `pk`.
A rule stored with the table and enforced by the DBMS on every insert, update, and delete.
The identifier for a row: unique, and not null on every engine except SQLite.
No duplicates allowed, nulls still permitted. Weaker than a primary key.
A condition every row must satisfy, best given a name so the error says which rule failed.
A column whose value must already exist in a parent table's key.
The state in which every foreign key value points at a row that exists.
7-7, the refused insert and the refused delete
The SQLite switch that turns foreign key enforcement on for the current connection. Off by default.
7-7, the two sandboxes side by side
A row whose foreign key points at a parent that is not there.

blocks.label: Data dictionary
blocks.text: Another name for the system catalog. Textbooks, Oracle documentation, and job postings all use it. If an interviewer asks how you would find every table containing a `CUSTOMER_NUM`, the answer they are listening for is the data dictionary, whatever the engine calls it.

One short check that ties the two halves of the module together. A constraint is not stored somewhere separate from the table; it is part of the table's definition, which means it is part of the catalog entry. Read the entry and you read the rules.

blocks.starter: SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = 'INVOICE_LINE';
blocks.solution:
SELECT name, sql
FROM sqlite_master
WHERE type = 'table'
  AND sql LIKE '%FOREIGN KEY%'
ORDER BY name;
blocks.hint: The `sql` column holds the text of the `CREATE TABLE`. Search that text for the words you care about.

blocks.text: The starter prints the whole definition of `INVOICE_LINE`, two-column primary key and both foreign keys included. The solution turns the same idea into an audit: `CUSTOMER`, `INVOICE`, and `INVOICE_LINE` declare a foreign key, and `ITEM` and `REP` do not, because nothing in this database sits above them.

The ten questions below are cumulative. Most of them come from 7-6 and 7-7, but several reach back to the joins, aggregates, nulls, subqueries, and `ALTER TABLE` work you have been doing since Module 4, because that is how this material arrives in practice. A constraint gets added and a query that used to work has to be checked. A table gets rebuilt and the catalog is the only place to confirm it. Read each scenario, decide before you look at the options, and read every note afterward, including the ones for answers you did not choose.

blocks.label: How to use the notes
blocks.text: Each wrong option has a note naming the specific mistake it stands for. Those mistakes are the ones that cost people real data, so the note is worth more than the checkmark. If a note describes something you would have done, go back to the section it came from before moving on.
Warm up in the sandbox first. This one puts a constrained table next to the shipped data, joins across, and then asks the catalog what it created, which is 7-6 and 7-7 in a single short script.

blocks.starter:
SELECT type, name, tbl_name
FROM sqlite_master
WHERE tbl_name = 'ITEM'
ORDER BY type;
blocks.hint: Build the table with a named `CHECK` and a foreign key, add two requests, join to `ITEM` for the descriptions, then count what the table put in the catalog. Keep the `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` so you can run it twice.

blocks.text: The join returns the grain-free dry food and the small animal grooming kit with their quantities. `CATALOG_ENTRIES` comes back as `2`: the table itself and the index SQLite built to enforce `REQUEST_ID`. The `CHECK` and the `FOREIGN KEY` did not add entries of their own, because they live inside the stored text of the `CREATE TABLE`, which the starter query showed you for `ITEM`.

blocks.text: Six exercises. The first four are on StayWell Student Accommodation, the last two return to KimTay Pet Supplies. Work each one in the sandbox before you open the solution. A sandbox keeps whatever you did to it until you press Reset, which reloads the sample data from scratch, so a mistake costs you nothing but one click. Every script below also carries the `DROP ... IF EXISTS` guards it needs to survive a second Run.

blocks.label: Read the data first
blocks.text: StayWell has two properties, Millbrook Commons (`P100`) managed by Diane Ortiz and Sycamore Court (`P200`) managed by Bruce Feldman, five rooms between them, four students, four leases, and four payments. Check the column names before you type: rooms carry `ROOM_TYPE`, `MONTHLY_RENT`, and `MAX_OCCUPANTS`, and `ROOM` has a two-column primary key of `PROPERTY_ID` and `ROOM_NUM`. Every column in every row is filled in.
Exercise 1: take inventory with the catalog

You have been handed the StayWell database with no documentation. List every table in it, then list the columns of `LEASE` with each column's type, whether it accepts nulls, and its position in the primary key. Run the starter before the solution and count how many entries are not tables.

blocks.starter: SELECT type, name FROM sqlite_master ORDER BY type, name;
blocks.solution:
SELECT type, name
FROM sqlite_master
WHERE type = 'table'
ORDER BY name;

SELECT name, type, "notnull", pk
FROM pragma_table_info('LEASE')
ORDER BY cid;
blocks.hint: `notnull` needs double quotation marks. Order by `cid` to get the columns in the order they were declared.

blocks.text: Eleven entries, of which six are tables and five are automatic primary-key indexes. `PAYMENT` has no index entry, and that is not a mistake: its key is `PAYMENT_ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, which SQLite stores as the row's own identifier, so no separate index is needed. `LEASE` comes back with seven columns and `pk` of `1` on `LEASE_ID` alone.
Exercise 2: create a view and an index, then find them in the catalog

StayWell wants a saved list of its double rooms, and searching by rent has become common enough to deserve an index. Create a view named `DOUBLE_ROOMS` over `ROOM` showing `PROPERTY_ID`, `ROOM_NUM`, and `MONTHLY_RENT` for rooms whose `ROOM_TYPE` is `Double`, create an index named `ROOM_RENT_IDX` on `ROOM (MONTHLY_RENT)`, prove both exist by reading the catalog, then list the view. Use `IF EXISTS` on the drops so the script survives a second run.

blocks.starter:
SELECT type, name, tbl_name
FROM sqlite_master
WHERE type IN ('view', 'index')
  AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'
ORDER BY type, name;
blocks.hint: The starter returns nothing at all, which is the point: this database ships with no views and no indexes of its own.

blocks.text: The catalog query returns two rows. Notice the `tbl_name` column: the index belongs to `ROOM`, while the view belongs to itself, because a view is not attached to any one table. The view lists the double at Millbrook Commons and the double at Sycamore Court, at 450 and 465.
Exercise 3: declare every constraint on a new table

StayWell is starting a room inspection programme, and the property managers do the inspecting. Build an `INSPECTION` table with `INSPECTION_ID` as the primary key, `PROPERTY_ID`, `ROOM_NUM`, `INSPECTOR`, and `SCORE` all required, a named `CHECK` keeping `SCORE` between 0 and 100, a named `UNIQUE` constraint allowing only one inspection per room, and a foreign key from the property and room pair to `ROOM`. Record `P100` room `101` inspected by Ortiz scoring 92 and `P200` room `202` inspected by Feldman scoring 88, list the table, then count what it added to the catalog.

blocks.hint: A constraint that covers two columns cannot live on a column line. Give it its own line after the last column, and a name.

blocks.text: Three catalog entries this time: the table, the index enforcing the primary key, and a second index enforcing `ONE_PER_ROOM`. The starter version has only two, because it declared no uniqueness beyond the key. That difference is the clearest evidence you will see that a `UNIQUE` constraint is a working structure and not a comment.
Exercise 4: prove referential integrity, twice

A lease is entered for student `S099`, who has never existed. Run the first sandbox with enforcement off, watch the orphan lease go in, then remove it. Then run the second, which turns enforcement on and attempts the identical insert. The second one is meant to fail, and the error is the answer.

blocks.starter: PRAGMA foreign_keys;
blocks.hint: Ask for the setting first. A `0` tells you what to expect from the insert that follows. The `DELETE` at the end tidies up, which is also what lets you press Run twice.

blocks.starter:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
PRAGMA foreign_keys;
blocks.solution:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

INSERT INTO LEASE VALUES ('L005', 'S099', 'P100', '101', '2026-08-15', '2027-05-15', 595.00);
blocks.hint: The starter proves the switch flipped. The solution is the same insert as the sandbox above, and it should now be refused.

blocks.text: With enforcement off the lease is accepted, five leases appear, and the join from `LEASE` to `STUDENT` silently returns four of them. With enforcement on the answer is `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` and nothing is written. The room part of the key was valid in both cases; `P100` room `101` exists. It was the missing student that stopped it.
Exercise 5: add a constraint to a table that already has rows

Back to KimTay. Nobody may be paid a commission rate above 0.25, and no commission total may be negative, but `REP` was created without either rule and SQLite has no `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT`. Rebuild `REP` with the pattern from 6-8a: create `REP_NEW` carrying the same nine columns plus a `NOT NULL` primary key, two named `CHECK` constraints, and a default of 0 for `COMMISSION`; copy the three reps across; drop the original; rename the replacement. Wrap it in a transaction, then confirm from the catalog that the rules are now part of the table.

blocks.starter: SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = 'REP';
blocks.hint: The starter shows the definition you are replacing. Copy it, add the rules, and remember that the `INSERT` will fail if any existing rep breaks one of them.

blocks.text: Kaiser, Hull, and Perez come through with rates of 0.05, 0.07, and 0.05, all inside the new range, which is why the copy succeeded. Read the final result carefully: the catalog now stores the rebuilt definition, with both named `CHECK` constraints in it, under the name `REP`, and the DBMS wrote that entry without being asked. Had one rep been on a rate of 0.30, the `INSERT` would have failed, the `COMMIT` would never have run, and the original table would still be there. That is why the transaction is not optional.
Exercise 6: audit the whole database from the catalog

A KimTay developer is planning to rename `ITEM_ID` and needs two facts before writing anything: how many columns each table has, and exactly which tables store a column called `ITEM_ID`. Produce both, with one query each, and do it without naming any table by hand except in the search itself.

blocks.starter: SELECT COUNT(*) AS COLUMN_COUNT FROM pragma_table_info('CUSTOMER');
blocks.solution:
SELECT m.name AS TABLE_NAME,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_table_info(m.name)) AS COLUMN_COUNT
FROM sqlite_master m
WHERE m.type = 'table'
ORDER BY m.name;

SELECT m.name AS TABLE_NAME
FROM sqlite_master m
WHERE m.type = 'table'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pragma_table_info(m.name) c WHERE c.name = 'ITEM_ID')
ORDER BY m.name;
blocks.hint: The starter counts one table's columns. Put that count in the select list of a query over `sqlite_master` and it runs once per table.

blocks.text: Nine columns in `CUSTOMER` and `REP`, six in `ITEM`, four in `INVOICE_LINE`, three in `INVOICE`. The second query names `INVOICE_LINE` and `ITEM`, so the rename is two statements and a check of every view and report that spelled the old name. Neither query mentions a table list you typed, which means both stay correct the day somebody adds a sixth table.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's inherited MySQL database
questions.stem: A contractor hands KimTay Pet Supplies a MySQL database and leaves. Before widening REP_NUM from two characters to three, the DBA has to know every table that stores a column named REP_NUM. Which approach produces that list reliably?
options: Run SELECT * on each table in turn and read the column headings that come back
Query INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS for every row whose COLUMN_NAME is REP_NUM
Run DESCRIBE REP and read the foreign key clauses printed underneath the columns
Search the application source code for the text REP_NUM and trust what it finds
optionNotes: This works only if you already know every table name, which is the thing you are trying to find out.
Correct: the COLUMNS table holds one row per column of every table, so a column name is searchable.
DESCRIBE reports the columns of the one table you name and says nothing about any other table.
Source code shows where a column is used, not where it is stored; an unused column still has to be changed.
questions.takeaway: The catalog is the only place that knows the whole schema, so schema questions go to the catalog.

questions.scenarioTitle: Listing views in the sandbox
questions.stem: An analyst working in the SQLite sandbox on this page wants a list of every view that exists in the current database. Which statement returns it?
options: SELECT TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS ORDER BY TABLE_NAME;
SHOW FULL TABLES WHERE Table_type = 'VIEW';
SELECT name FROM pragma_table_info('VIEWS') ORDER BY name;
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view' ORDER BY name;
optionNotes: INFORMATION_SCHEMA is MySQL's catalog and does not exist in SQLite at any version.
SHOW is a MySQL command over its own catalog; SQLite has no SHOW statement to run.
pragma_table_info takes a table name and returns its columns, and there is no table called VIEWS.
Correct: sqlite_master holds one row per object, and type tells you whether it is a table, view, index, or trigger.
questions.takeaway: One catalog table, filtered by type, answers every what-exists question in SQLite.

questions.scenarioTitle: The audit table that registered itself
questions.stem: A DBA at KimTay runs CREATE TABLE AUDIT_LOG, then immediately queries sqlite_master and finds a row describing AUDIT_LOG already there. Who put that row in the catalog?
options: The DBMS wrote it while carrying out the CREATE TABLE statement itself
The DBA must run an INSERT into sqlite_master to register any new table
Nothing was written; the sandbox rebuilds the catalog by scanning the file each time
A background job refreshes the catalog on a schedule, so the entry may lag behind
optionNotes: Correct: updating the catalog is part of executing the statement, so the two can never disagree.
Writing to the catalog by hand is refused with 'table sqlite_master may not be modified', and on engines that permit it the result is a corrupt database.
The catalog is stored, not derived; dropping the table is what removes the row, not a rescan.
There is no delay and no scheduled refresh; the entry exists the moment the statement finishes.
questions.takeaway: CREATE, ALTER, and DROP update the catalog as part of their own work, which is why it is never stale.

questions.scenarioTitle: Whiskers and Wags Boutique, entered twice
questions.stem: A clerk at KimTay accidentally runs the insert for customer 1420, Whiskers and Wags Boutique, a second time. CUSTOMER_NUM is the primary key of CUSTOMER. What happens?
options: NOT NULL refuses the row, and the second copy is stored with a null customer number
CHECK refuses it because 1420 falls outside the range allowed for that column
The primary key refuses it, the insert is rejected, and the table is left unchanged
Nothing refuses it, and the second row quietly overwrites the first one in the table
optionNotes: NOT NULL is about missing values, and a rejected insert never stores a partial row anywhere.
No CHECK constraint is declared on CUSTOMER_NUM, and a duplicate is not a range problem.
Correct: a primary key forbids duplicate values, so the engine rejects the statement outright.
An INSERT never replaces an existing row; that would silently destroy the data already stored.
questions.takeaway: A primary key is a promise of uniqueness that the DBMS keeps on every insert, without being asked.

questions.scenarioTitle: Retiring the grain-free dry food
questions.stem: KimTay runs on MySQL with InnoDB. A buyer tries to delete item CF21 from ITEM, and CF21 still appears on invoice lines for 50710 and 50711. What does the engine do?
options: It refuses the delete, because invoice lines still reference CF21 as their item
It performs the delete and repoints the two invoice lines at the next item alphabetically
It performs the delete, because a foreign key restricts inserts into the child table only
It performs the delete and removes the two invoice lines along with the parent item
optionNotes: Correct: referential integrity guards the parent too, so the delete is rejected while children exist.
No engine invents a replacement value; that would silently change what the invoices say was sold.
A foreign key constrains both sides: children may not point at nothing, and parents may not vanish.
That happens only when the foreign key was declared ON DELETE CASCADE, which is a deliberate choice.
questions.takeaway: Referential integrity blocks deletes as well as inserts, because both can leave a foreign key pointing at nothing.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two students, one sandbox, two results
questions.stem: In the sandbox on this page, one student inserts an invoice line for item ZZ99, which does not exist, and the row is accepted. A classmate runs the identical insert and it is refused with FOREIGN KEY constraint failed. What explains the difference?
options: The classmate is on a newer SQLite version in which foreign keys became mandatory
The first insert was inside an uncommitted transaction, so that row is not really stored
The classmate's copy of INVOICE_LINE is missing the FOREIGN KEY clause entirely
The classmate ran PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, which enables enforcement for that connection
optionNotes: Enforcement has been optional in every SQLite version and is still off by default in this sandbox.
Both sandboxes run outside an explicit transaction, and the accepted row is genuinely in the table.
Having the clause is what makes enforcement possible; without it the pragma would change nothing.
Correct: SQLite stores foreign keys always but enforces them only when the pragma is on for the connection.
questions.takeaway: In SQLite a declared foreign key and an enforced foreign key are two different things, separated by one pragma.

questions.scenarioTitle: Capping a KimTay commission rate
questions.stem: KimTay decides no sales rep may ever be recorded on a commission rate above 0.25. Reps are added by a web form, by a nightly import, and occasionally by hand at a command line. Where does the rule belong?
options: In the web form's validation code, so the check runs before the database is ever contacted
As a CHECK constraint on REP, so every program and every person is held to the same rule
In a nightly report listing rates above 0.25 so somebody can correct them the next morning
As a NOT NULL constraint on RATE, which stops any out-of-range value from being stored
optionNotes: Validation in the form protects only the form, and here there are three ways in, not one.
Correct: a constraint in the table is enforced on every statement from every source, permanently.
A report finds bad data after it is stored and after decisions have been made on it.
NOT NULL only requires a value to be present; 0.90 is present and would be accepted.
questions.takeaway: A rule that matters belongs in the table, because the table outlives every application that writes to it.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two questions about Access Pet Center
questions.stem: A KimTay analyst has two questions: what balance is stored for Access Pet Center, and what type and size the BALANCE column was declared with. Which statement about answering them is correct?
options: Both are catalog questions, because the catalog stores column values as well as definitions
Both are data questions, because a SELECT on CUSTOMER returns the type along with the value
The balance comes from the data and the column definition comes from the catalog
Neither can be answered without administrator rights on the underlying MySQL server
optionNotes: The catalog records structure only; it has never held a single customer balance.
A SELECT returns values, and the column headings, but not the declared type or size.
Correct: values live in the table, definitions live in the catalog, and each answers its own kind of question.
Reading your own tables and your own catalog entries needs no special privilege at all.
questions.takeaway: Values come from the table; types, sizes, and null settings come from the catalog.

questions.scenarioTitle: The invoice line that disappears from a join
questions.stem: With foreign key enforcement off, someone inserts an INVOICE_LINE row for item ZZ99. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE_LINE returns 7, but the same count over INVOICE_LINE inner joined to ITEM returns 6. What has happened?
options: The orphan row has no matching item, so the inner join leaves it out of the result
The join is broken and should be rewritten, because a count must match on both sides
COUNT(*) skips nulls in the join and therefore reports one row fewer than it should
The insert was rolled back automatically, so the seventh row does not really exist
optionNotes: Correct: an inner join keeps only matched rows, so a row pointing at nothing silently vanishes.
The join is written correctly; the mismatch is a data problem the join is exposing, not causing.
COUNT(*) counts rows and ignores nulls in columns entirely; the join lost the row, not the count.
Nothing was rolled back: with enforcement off the row was accepted and is in the table.
questions.takeaway: Orphan rows do not announce themselves; they show up as counts that quietly refuse to agree.

questions.scenarioTitle: Reading the catalog entry for INVOICE_LINE
questions.stem: Running SELECT name, type, "notnull", pk FROM pragma_table_info('INVOICE_LINE') returns pk values of 1 for INVOICE_NUM, 2 for ITEM_ID, and 0 for the other two columns. What does that describe?
options: Two separate primary keys on the table, one ranked above the other in importance
A primary key on INVOICE_NUM and a foreign key on ITEM_ID, numbered in that order
A primary key on INVOICE_NUM only, with ITEM_ID as the second most indexed column
One primary key made of two columns, INVOICE_NUM first and ITEM_ID second
optionNotes: A table has exactly one primary key; there is no ranking of several keys.
pk numbers key position, not key kind; foreign keys do not appear in this column at all.
The 2 would be 0 if ITEM_ID were outside the key, and pk says nothing about indexing.
Correct: the numbers give each column's position within the single composite primary key.
questions.takeaway: In pragma_table_info, pk is a position inside the primary key, and any value above zero means the column is part of it.

questions.scenarioTitle: Cleaning up the KimTay archive table
questions.stem: A DBA created ITEM_ARCHIVE with a primary key and then added an index on its PRICE column, taking the catalog from 10 entries to 13. She now runs DROP TABLE ITEM_ARCHIVE. What does the catalog hold afterward?
options: 12 entries, because the index she created survives the table it was built on
10 entries, because dropping a table removes its own index entries as well
11 entries, because the automatic primary-key index is kept for possible reuse
13 entries, because DROP TABLE empties a table but leaves its definition in place
optionNotes: An index cannot exist without its table; it is removed with the table, not left behind.
Correct: all three entries belonged to ITEM_ARCHIVE, so all three go when the table goes.
Nothing about an index is kept for reuse; the entry describes a structure that no longer exists.
DROP TABLE removes structure and rows together; DELETE is the statement that empties a table.
questions.takeaway: Dropping a table takes every catalog entry that belonged to it, indexes included.

questions.scenarioTitle: A late rule for KimTay's prices
questions.stem: KimTay wants PRICE > 0 enforced on the existing ITEM table, which already holds five rows. The database is SQLite. What has to happen?
options: Run ALTER TABLE ITEM ADD CONSTRAINT PRICE_POSITIVE CHECK (PRICE > 0) as written
Add the rule to every program that inserts items, since SQLite has no CHECK at all
Recreate the whole database from scratch, because constraints cannot be added later
Rebuild the table: create a replacement declaring the CHECK, copy the rows, drop, rename
optionNotes: SQLite has no ADD CONSTRAINT at any version; it expects a column definition after ADD and answers 'near "CONSTRAINT": syntax error'.
SQLite supports CHECK fully; what it lacks is a way to attach one after the table exists.
Only the one table has to be rebuilt, and the copy pattern from 6-8a does it inside a transaction.
Correct: create, copy, drop, rename, all in one transaction, is the portable way to add a constraint.
questions.takeaway: On SQLite a constraint has to be present at creation, so adding one means rebuilding that one table.

questions.scenarioTitle: A refused supplier at KimTay
questions.stem: Inside an open transaction, a clerk inserts two valid suppliers and then a third whose LEAD_DAYS is 0, which a named CHECK refuses. What is the state of things immediately after the error?
options: All three inserts are undone, because one failure rolls back the entire transaction at once
The third row is stored with LEAD_DAYS set to null, so the constraint has something legal
The two valid rows are still pending, the third changed nothing, and the transaction is open
The table is locked until an administrator clears the violation from the constraint log
optionNotes: A rejected statement undoes itself, not the whole transaction; the earlier work is still yours to commit.
Refusing a row means storing nothing; the engine never substitutes a value to make a row fit.
Correct: the failed INSERT changed nothing at all, and you may still COMMIT or ROLLBACK the rest.
There is no constraint log and no lock; the error is returned to you and the database moves on.
questions.takeaway: A constraint violation cancels one statement completely and leaves the surrounding transaction in your hands.

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep nobody can find
questions.stem: A practice table is created in the sandbox with REP_NUM CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY, and an insert supplying NULL for REP_NUM is accepted. COUNT(*) returns 1 and COUNT(REP_NUM) returns 0. What is going on, and what is the fix?
options: SQLite does not force a primary key column to be NOT NULL, so declare NOT NULL yourself
COUNT(REP_NUM) is the wrong function here; the key is present but excluded from counting
The primary key was silently dropped because CHAR(2) cannot serve as a key in SQLite
The row is invisible to other queries and will be removed the next time the table is read
optionNotes: Correct: SQLite allows this for backward compatibility, and NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY closes the hole.
COUNT(column) skipping nulls is exactly right; it is what proves no key value was stored.
The key is declared and working; it is only the null that SQLite failed to refuse.
The row is perfectly visible and permanent; nothing removes it on its own.
questions.takeaway: MySQL and Oracle make a primary key NOT NULL for you; on SQLite you write the two words yourself.

questions.scenarioTitle: An email column for KimTay suppliers
questions.stem: KimTay wants no two suppliers to share an email address, but a supplier that has not given one yet must still be storable. Which constraint fits?
options: PRIMARY KEY on EMAIL, since it is unique and every table needs a key on its most searched column
UNIQUE on EMAIL, which forbids duplicate addresses while still allowing the column to be null
NOT NULL on EMAIL, which prevents two suppliers from ending up with the same address
CHECK (EMAIL <> EMAIL) on the column, which the engine evaluates once per inserted row
optionNotes: A primary key identifies the row and would refuse the missing addresses you have to allow.
Correct: UNIQUE is the rule for no duplicates, and unlike a primary key it tolerates nulls.
NOT NULL requires a value to be present and says nothing whatever about duplicates.
A CHECK sees one row at a time and can never compare a value against other rows in the table.
questions.takeaway: UNIQUE is the constraint for no duplicates when the value may legitimately be missing.

questions.scenarioTitle: A view that updates itself at Downtown Aquarium and Pets
questions.stem: A view over CUSTOMER selects the customers with a balance above 1000 and returns three rows. A new customer is then inserted with a balance of 5000. Without anyone touching the view, it now returns four rows. Why?
options: The view stored a copy of the three rows and appended the fourth when the insert committed
CREATE VIEW builds an index that the engine refreshes whenever the base table changes
A view stores its defining query, which the DBMS runs again every time the view is used
The view is out of date and will keep growing until somebody drops and recreates it
optionNotes: A view holds no rows of its own, so there is no stored copy for anything to be appended to.
A view is not an index and creating one builds no structure over the base table at all.
Correct: the query runs at use time against current data, which is why a view is never stale.
Returning the fourth row is the view being right, not the view drifting out of date.
questions.takeaway: A view is a stored query, not stored data, so it always reflects the table as it is right now.

questions.scenarioTitle: Retiring an aviary cage at KimTay
questions.stem: With foreign keys enforced, KimTay wants item AV07 gone. AV07 appears on one line of invoice 50712. Which sequence completes without violating a constraint?
options: Delete the invoice line for AV07 first, then delete AV07 from ITEM
Delete AV07 from ITEM first, then delete the invoice line that referenced it
Delete AV07 from ITEM, since the engine removes any dependent invoice lines by default
Delete neither; a row referenced by a foreign key can never be removed on any engine
optionNotes: Correct: remove the child rows first and the parent then has nothing pointing at it.
This is refused: while the line exists, deleting the item would leave it pointing at nothing.
Cascading happens only when the foreign key was declared ON DELETE CASCADE, which this one was not.
It can be removed; the rule is about order, and clearing the children first is what makes it legal.
questions.takeaway: Referential integrity does not forbid deletions, it dictates their order: children first, then the parent.

matchers.heading: 🧩 Match the rule to the constraint that enforces it
matchers.prompt: Each card states a rule KimTay Pet Supplies wants the database itself to keep. Drop it on the constraint that enforces exactly that rule and nothing wider. Every card fits one zone only.

cards.text: REP_NUM is what identifies one rep, so it may be neither missing nor repeated
cards.why: Requiring both uniqueness and presence, and naming the identifier, is exactly what a primary key declares.

cards.text: CUSTOMER_NUM tells you which customer a row is about and can never be blank or duplicated
cards.why: It is the identifier of the row, so the constraint that covers uniqueness and presence together is the primary key.

cards.text: Two suppliers may not share an email address, though a supplier may have none on file
cards.why: No duplicates but nulls still permitted is the difference between UNIQUE and a primary key.

cards.text: A rep's LAST_NAME must always be filled in, whatever else about the rep is unknown
cards.why: The rule is only that a value must be present; nothing here says the surnames have to differ.

cards.text: A commission rate has to fall between 0 and 0.25 for every rep on the payroll
cards.why: A condition tested against the value in the row is what a CHECK expression evaluates.

cards.text: An item's ON_HAND count may never be recorded as a negative number
cards.why: It is a range test on one column's value, so a CHECK is the constraint that refuses it.

cards.text: An invoice line may only name an item that already exists in the ITEM table
cards.why: A value that has to be found in a parent table's key is a foreign key, which is referential integrity.

cards.text: Deleting item CF21 must be refused while invoice lines still point at it
cards.why: Protecting a parent row from deletion while children reference it is the other half of a foreign key's job.

matchers.heading: 🧩 Sort the Module 7 Terms
matchers.prompt: Each card describes one thing a database professional relied on this week. Drop it into the part of Module 7 it belongs to. Every card fits exactly one zone.

cards.text: A stored SELECT over three columns of CUSTOMER that people query by name, as though it were a table of its own
cards.why: Saving a query under a name and using it like a table is the definition of a view.

cards.text: Holding no rows of its own, because its defining query runs again on every use
cards.why: Storing a query rather than data is the defining property of a view.

cards.text: Letting the engine find every customer of rep 65 without reading the whole table
cards.why: Locating rows by a column value without a full scan is precisely what an index provides.

cards.text: Something the DBMS also builds by itself to enforce every primary key you declare
cards.why: The sqlite_autoindex entries in the catalog are indexes created automatically to keep keys unique.

cards.text: The entries that record which tables, views, and indexes exist in this database
cards.why: Recording what objects exist and how they are defined is the whole purpose of the system catalog.

cards.text: Where both pragma_table_info and INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS get their answers
cards.why: Both are engine-specific windows onto the same thing: the database's record of its own structure.

cards.text: Refusing an invoice line that names an item which does not exist in ITEM
cards.why: A rule the DBMS applies to every insert, rejecting the statement outright, is an integrity constraint.

cards.text: What GRANT hands to a named user and REVOKE takes back again on MySQL
cards.why: A privilege is the specific right on a specific object that those two statements move around.

sqlChecks.expect: One row per table in the KIMTAY database: CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, ITEM, REP. Not runnable in the sandbox; INFORMATION_SCHEMA does not exist in SQLite.

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT COLUMN_NAME, DATA_TYPE, CHARACTER_MAXIMUM_LENGTH, IS_NULLABLE FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY' AND TABLE_NAME = 'REP' ORDER BY ORDINAL_POSITION;
sqlChecks.expect: Nine rows, one per column of REP, in declaration order; LAST_NAME and FIRST_NAME show IS_NULLABLE of NO.

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT type, name FROM sqlite_master ORDER BY type, name;

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT type, name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type IN ('table', 'view') ORDER BY type, name;

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT name, type FROM pragma_table_info('REP') ORDER BY cid;

sqlChecks.expect: 5 rows: CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, ITEM, REP (table-comparison row, SQLite column).

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT name FROM pragma_table_info('REP');
sqlChecks.expect: 9 rows, the column names of REP (table-comparison row, SQLite column).

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view';
sqlChecks.expect: 0 rows on the shipped data; the database contains no views until one is created (table-comparison row, SQLite column).

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index';
sqlChecks.expect: 5 rows, the automatic primary-key indexes sqlite_autoindex_CUSTOMER_1, _INVOICE_1, _INVOICE_LINE_1, _ITEM_1, _REP_1 (table-comparison row, SQLite column).

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY';
sqlChecks.expect: The five KimTay table names (table-comparison row, MySQL column).

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'KIMTAY' AND TABLE_NAME = 'REP';
sqlChecks.expect: The nine column names of REP. The TABLE_SCHEMA filter matters: without it the query also returns REP columns from any other database on the server (table-comparison row, MySQL column).

sqlChecks.expect: One row per index in KIMTAY, including the PRIMARY entry MySQL creates for each primary key. DISTINCT is needed because STATISTICS holds one row per indexed column, not per index (table-comparison row, MySQL column).
